articles.title: Two people sentenced to 60 and 45 years in prison in death of Telemundo reporter
articles.summary:
Danette Colbert and Rickey White sentenced in Adan Manzano’s death for racketeering and negligent homicide

A Louisiana judge has…

blocks.text: A Louisiana judge has handed lengthy prison sentences to two people convicted of roles in a criminal enterprise that targeted New Orleans tourists led to the death of a reporter covering the 2025 Super Bowl there.

Nancy Miller, a state court judge, on Monday sentenced Danette Colbert, 49, to a total of 60 years in prison: fifty years for racketeering and a consecutive 10 years for negligent homicide in the death of Adan Manzano, a journalist for the Spanish-language news outlet Telemundo Kansas City.
Colbert’s accomplice, Rickey White, was sentenced to 45 years’ imprisonment for racketeering.

The sentences come just days after a jury in the suburban New Orleans community of Jefferson parish, Louisiana, convicted both Colbert and White, 35, for their roles in the 5 February 2025 death of Manzano, 27.

Manzano had traveled to the New Orleans area to cover the Kansas City Chiefs’ Super Bowl clash with the Philadelphia Eagles. He was found dead in his hotel room in Kenner, Louisiana, the suburb where New Orleans’ international airport is, days before the Chiefs lost the big game to the Eagles.
The Jefferson parish coroner’s office, whose jurisdiction includes Kenner, said Manzano died from positional asphyxiation. An autopsy found Xanax and alcohol in his system.

Prosecutors said Manzano was among the victims of a yearslong operation in which Colbert, White and a co-defendant who testified against them – Christian Anderson – targeted unsuspecting tourists in the city’s French Quarter. The group allegedly lured victims with the promise of sex before drugging and robbing them.
Prosecutors said the criminal enterprise dated back to 2012.

Manzano’s father addressed his son’s death at Monday’s sentencing via a videoconferencing platform. According to a statement from Jefferson parish district attorney Paul Connick’s office, Manzano’s father called the sentencing “a say day for me and my family”.
“May the laws of this country lock up the people that destroyed my life,” he testified. “I respectfully ask that you give them the sentencing they deserve.”
According to local news channel WVUE, the father added: “They snatched his dreams, life and family as we were seeing him happy and successful.”
Manzano’s mother, meanwhile, said: “I don’t want to say anything to the people that committed this crime, because they are beings of darkness, beings that don’t have God in their lives.

“But I don’t think they should go on with life causing harm and killing people – because I still can’t accept that Adan is not here … This loss, I’ll never overcome it. I don’t wish this on anybody, on any family.”

A cousin of Manzano, Carlos Castillo, reportedly said: “I want to look you guys in the face and say that you should pay your entire life for this … Every time the cell opens and you cannot see the light, you think of my cousin.”

Manzano’s wife, Ashleigh Boyd, was killed in an April 2024 car crash in Topeka, Kansas. A Topeka judge found Todd W Armstrong guilty of vehicular homicide, speeding and driving on the wrong side of the road after a one-day trial on 21 September, four days after the jury verdict in Manzano’s death in Louisiana.
Boyd and Manzano’s daughter – Eleanor, now three – is being raised by her maternal grandparents.
Months after Manzano’s death, Colbert received a 25-year prison sentence for being found to have violated her probation on a prior theft and fraud conviction and being classified a habitual offender.
Miller on Monday told Colbert that her “behavior in this matter [is] quite alarming”, according to WVUE.

“You were indifferent to the impact that your actions had,” Miller said. “That is evident by your consistent pattern in your criminal history. Apparently, you’ve been doing this for quite some time. It’s finally caught up to you with the death of one of your victims.”

articles.title: New tool directly links carbon emissions to amount of environmental and economic damage caused
articles.summary:
Carbon Impacts Tracer can be used to estimate climate impact from emissions across eight different factors, including lost food production

The biggest coal project before authorities in New…
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: The biggest coal project before authorities in New South Wales, the HVO mine, will emit the equivalent of about 809m tonnes of climate-warming carbon dioxide if it wins approval.
That number, for most people, will carry little meaning, as might the calculation that adding that amount of greenhouse gas to the atmosphere will cause an extra 0.00036C of global heating.

But what if the public was instead told that that amount of carbon dioxide would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, or kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches?
All those statistics come from a new tool that translates the emissions from burning fossil fuels into estimated real-world climate effects taken from peer-reviewed climate studies.

“Small numbers in global warming can mean catastrophic impacts,” says prof Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick, a climate scientist at the Australian National University who is part of a team launching the Carbon Impacts Tracer.

The NSW Independent Planning Commission is expected to make a decision this week about the future of the HVO mine, with the joint owners Yancoal and Glencore hoping to keep digging at the Hunter Valley site until 2045.

Plugging the project’s expected emissions into the tracer suggests, for example, the extra heat trapped in the atmosphere by its emissions will reduce crop production every year by an amount that is the equivalent to the minimum dietary requirements of 276,129 people.

The tool can be used to estimate the impact of carbon dioxide emissions from any project, company or state – or for any known amount of emissions – across eight different factors including the loss of labour hours due to excess heat, the loss of glaciers, the death of corals or lost food production.
Central to the tool is a metric known as Transient Climate Response to CO₂ Emissions (TCRE) – an established calculation that every billion tonnes of CO2 causes about 0.45C of global heating.

Once an amount of CO2 is known – such as from a major fossil project – it’s contribution to global heating can be calculated and, from there, says Perkins-Kirkpatrick, measured against already published studies.
“Every tonne of CO2 maters and we’ve known this for decades,” she said.

“To pinpoint what this means with a high degree of confidence has taken us a long time. This [tool] is to hold big fossil fuel emitters accountable. It is not meant to be a blame game. It just shows that all emissions have impacts and now we can prove it.”
All the results are presented as the best estimate within a likely range of uncertainty, with links back to the original scientific studies used for the calculations.
Perkins-Kirkpatrick accepts some may be sceptical of the results, but counters “we are not making these numbers up for shits and giggles.”
“This is based on the best analysis published in the peer-reviewed literature,” she said. “
And this is only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the impacts [of fossil fuel burning].”

The Carbon Impacts Tracer was developed by scientists at the Australian National University, the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century and the Lethal Humidity Global Council, and was funded by the Minderoo Foundation.
Maria Nawaz leads the Australian Climate Accountability Project at the Australian Human Rights Institute at the University of New South Wales – a partner in the tracer project.
“One of the major challenges in climate litigation has been establishing a direct link between a government or a corporation’s actions and climate harms and suffering,” she said.
“Governments and corporations have argued their emissions are ‘just a drop in the ocean’ and too small to measure.
“But we can now refute this defence and show the emissions of any state or corporation can be tied to a global warming figure and then human and ecological harms. It is transformative.”

Elaine Johnson, an experienced climate lawyer and director of Johnson Legal but not involved in the work, said there will be governments and corporations that will not welcome the development of the tool.
“Fossil fuel companies do not want people to be able to make that connection between their products and, say, deaths from heatwaves.
“But now the science is at the point where we can make those connections clearly. That is a story the industry does not want told.”
The Guardian approached Glencore, a partner in the HVO mine, for comment, but received no response.

articles.title: Canada did not see historic population decline last year, StatsCan says after second look
articles.summary: Canada's population saw a slight bump in 2025, Statistics Canada says, revising a previous estimate that showed the population decreased for the first time in the country's history.

image.caption: Canada's population saw an increase of 280,810 last year, according to revised federal data. (Brian Morris/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Canada's population saw a slight bump in 2025, Statistics Canada says, revising a previous estimate that showed the population decreased for the first time in the country's history.
Preliminary numbers suggested population decreased for first time in Canada's history
The statistics agency released new numbers last week that suggest the population grew slightly, by 280,810 people, in all of 2025.
The new estimate is a revision from data released in March that indicated the country had seen an annual net decline in residents for the first time since Confederation.

"These estimates were preliminary and Statistics Canada indicated at the time that upcoming updates could be larger than usual and that the estimated population decrease could become an increase as more complete administrative data became available," a Statistics Canada spokesperson said in an email.
The agency said in March that the initial estimate should be treated "with caution" because work and study permit extensions could "lead to larger than usual updates" in the future.
Growth still slow, StatsCan says
The agency said the revised estimate still indicates a significant slowdown in population growth.
The government under former prime minister Justin Trudeau began cutting back on both permanent and temporary immigration after it rapidly increased during the post-pandemic labour shortage.
Prior to Prime Minister Mark Carney taking office, the Liberals had already taken steps to shrink temporary residents' share of Canada's population.
Carney's first budget said Canada would admit only 385,000 temporary residents in 2026 — about 43 per cent fewer than the 2025 target — and 370,000 in 2027 and 2028.
The budget also said that the federal government would limit the number of new permanent residents to 380,000 annually between 2026 and 2028.

A Dutch man whose journey from cybercriminal to reformed security professional was widely covered in the international media has been arrested ‌as part of an investigation into the hacker group ShinyHunters, Dutch police and the man's boss said on Monday. The arrest of the 24-year-old 'reformed hacker' left his boss 'flabbergasted'

A Dutch man whose journey from cybercriminal to reformed security professional was widely covered in the international media has been arrested ‌as part of an investigation into the hacker group ShinyHunters, Dutch police and the man's boss said on Monday.
In a statement posted to the social media site X, Dutch police said that a ​24-year-old man had been arrested in connection with the ​inquiry and would appear in court in Rotterdam on Tuesday.

The statement did not identify the man by name, but ​his boss, Benjamin Korper of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security, said it ⁠was Pepijn van ⁠der Stap, the company's offensive security ‌lead.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, Korper said his office was visited by Dutch forensic investigators on Sept. 15, the same night Van der Stap was arrested in a police raid.

Van der Stap's ⁠2023 convictions on data theft and extortion charges received widespread publicity, as did his subsequent disavowal of cybercrime. Korper said he had carefully vetted Van der Stap before hiring him ‌and was shocked by the arrest.

articles.title: TikTok, X reportedly barring ads for documentary about Elon Musk
articles.summary: Ads for a documentary about controversial billionaire Elon Musk have reportedly been banned from both TikTok and X but, after brief delays, are now running on YouTube and Meta's social media…

image.caption: Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, attends the Viva Technology conference in Paris, on June 16, 2023. (Gonzalo Fuentes/File Photo/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Ads for a documentary about controversial billionaire Elon Musk have reportedly been banned from both TikTok and X but, after brief delays, are now running on YouTube and Meta's social media platforms.
YouTube, Meta say ads for Musk now running after brief delays

Ads for a documentary putting a critical lens on controversial billionaire Elon Musk have reportedly been banned from both TikTok and X but, after brief delays, are now running on YouTube and Meta's social media platforms.
The trailer for the nearly four-hour film Musk dropped on Thursday ahead of its Oct. 9 theatrical release.

But on Friday, a story in the Hollywood Reporter said indie distributor Bleecker Street was rejected by all four companies when it attempted to buy ads on the platforms for the film. YouTube, TikTok and Meta — parent company to Facebook and Instagram — reportedly blamed its "political content" while X, which Musk owns, did not comment.
In the wake of an online backlash, YouTube said on Saturday that ads for Musk are now running on the platform.
"When submitted as an ad, it was temporarily restricted by our system," YouTube said through its updates account on X. "Following review the ad has been cleared to run."
A spokesperson for Meta told CBC News on Monday that the ads "were rejected in error and have been restored," without elaborating.
Bleecker Street, TikTok and X did not return calls for comment.

TikTok does not permit paid political ads, and Meta restricts them in some regions such as the European Union. YouTube allows political ads with transparency disclosures, and X permits them in regions including the U.S.

Musk's political profile rose sharply when he campaigned for U.S. President Donald Trump's re-election in 2024 and ultimately joined his administration as head of the budget-slashing Department of Government Efficiency. He has since left the administration, but remains a divisive and outspoken figure.
But while Musk's trailer includes brief clips from his appearances on the campaign trail, it's unclear how this would qualify it as the type of campaign ads covered by platforms' restrictions.

One of the topics of the film is how the richest man in the world has allegedly aimed to control conversation online — digging into his purchase of Twitter, now X, and allegations that Musk, despite his free-speech stylings, may have used his Starlink satellites to improperly influence the 2024 election.
'Censorious platforms'
After YouTube and Meta said they had OK'd the ads, director Alex Gibney said the "public pressure worked."
"The censorious platforms backed down,” he wrote Saturday on X.

Gibney later posted a 2022 quote from a Musk press release about his acquisition of Twitter, in which he stated "free speech is the bedrock of a functioning democracy, and Twitter is the digital town square where matters vital to the future of humanity are debated."
"Will X allow ads for the trailer for my film 'Musk,' about the self-proclaimed 'free-speech absolutist?'" he wrote.
Since 2023, when Gibney announced his intent to make the film, Musk has consistently called it a "hit piece."

He called Gibney "a horrible human" and "a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago" on X in the wake of the film’s debut at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month. He also reportedly threatened the production with legal action over its insinuations about the Starlink satellites.
The film has been widely praised by critics.

Musk isn't the only tech billionaire coming under the camera this year. Aaron Sorkin's dramatized The Social Reckoning, a followup to 2010's The Social Network, which Sorkin wrote, which puts the spotlight on Mark Zuckerberg, will be released by Sony next month.

articles.title: Trump unveils plan for $15bn Iowa steel plant he calls biggest in US history
articles.summary:
President seeks midterms boost as White House says project, built by Indian-owned company, will begin in 2030

Donald Trump on Monday announced what he called the largest steel plant in…

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Monday announced what he called the largest steel plant in American history to be built in Iowa, giving Republicans a jobs message to take to voters in a state that could help decide control of the Senate in November.

“Using advanced steelmaking technology, the plant will produce some of the highest quality, most affordable steel anywhere in the world,” Trump said in the Oval Office, flanked by Iowa’s top Republicans.

The plant, which “they’ve already started building”, Trump said, will be built in eastern Iowa by the foreign-owned steelmaker Mesabi Metallics and is expected to cost about $15bn, according to a White House official. It aims to begin production in 2030, years after voters go to the polls in November.

In his announcement, Trump singled out Iowa’s Ashley Hinson, the Republican congresswoman who was in the Oval Office and who is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Joni Ernst, also in the room. “I saw some good polls just recently,” he told her. “Looks like you’re doing well.”

But the polls for that race are less rosy than Trump suggested. A Marist survey published last week found Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by eight points in the conservative state, while an earlier Emerson College poll had Hinson narrowly ahead but found voters worried about tariffs. Democrats see the seat as one of four they need to retake the Senate.

Trump said the plant would run on iron ore from the company’s mine in Minnesota, which accounted for roughly 60% of iron ore production in the US in the 20th century. The president took the chance to attack that state’s Democratic governor, Tim Walz.

“They have one of the worst governors in history, a real stupid guy, but they do have good iron ore, which is more important, I guess,” Trump said. The two men have clashed over mining in the state, most recently over Walz’s August order halting permitting for mining projects near the Boundary Waters wilderness.

The Mesabi Metallics company itself, however, is owned by the India-based Essar Group, and US taxpayers are helping to pay for the expansion: the Export-Import Bank, a federal agency, will provide up to $10bn in financing.

When asked whether global outsourcing would be needed to build the plant, the chairman of Mesabi Metallics, Rewant Ruia, said “most of the critical materials” would come from the US but added “there are some materials that might be used that need to be imported for making and refining the highest quality steels”.

Still, the president credited his tariffs – the taxes the US charges consumers on imported goods – for the investment. “Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs,” he said. “It’s really not that complicated. A lot of people say they don’t understand it, but they do. They just don’t like to give us credit.”
Trump said the project was “expected to create up to 6,000 new construction jobs, nearly 2,000 manufacturing and mining jobs, and add another $95bn to the US economy”.

articles.title: Judge sets $5m bond for third suspect in killing of Black woman hung from tree in Mississippi
articles.summary:
Police said Tasia Fortune, 29, was killed before her body was placed in the tree, and the scene was ‘staged’

A Mississippi judge…

blocks.text: A Mississippi judge set a $5m bond on Monday for a third man charged in the death of a Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in August.
Police disclosed on Friday that Tasia Fortune, 29, was killed before her body was placed in a tree behind an abandoned house in Jackson, Mississippi’s capital city.

Fortune was Black, and the discovery of her hanging body stoked fear because the scene recalled actual lynchings in Mississippi, a southern US state with a long history of racial violence. Some officials had called for a federal civil rights investigation before a Jackson police detective said the scene was “staged”.
“People justifiably didn’t know if we had a killer on the loose who might hang people for racial reasons,” judge Jeffery Reynolds said Monday.
He said it was a “heinous” act that shocked Jackson.

Reynolds presided at a hearing for Eric Clark, 45, who turned himself in on Friday. The Hinds county public defender’s office, which is representing him, declined to comment. Clark and two other men charged in Fortune’s death – Jarques Ratliff and Earnest Lloyd Jr – are Black.
Ratliff and Lloyd Jr have been denied bond.

Outside court on Monday, RaShall Brackney, Jackson police chief, repeated what was disclosed at a hearing on Friday, telling reporters that Fortune was killed as a result of a dispute over drugs. The body was discovered in a tree on 3 August.
Brackney said props were left at the scene “as part of the staging” of a hanging and – as she has remarked before – that more arrests were likely.
Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, said Clark approached her following a hearing for co-defendant Ratliff and hugged her at the courthouse.
“He never said he did it, but he said he was there to turn himself in for murder,” Spivey told reporters on Monday.
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title: Local representatives question official accounts after suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford
articles.summary:
Amid conflicting statements, local MP and councillors demand answers over how suspects were allowed to enter residential areas of nearby village

An MP and councillors representing the…

blocks.text: An MP and councillors representing the residents of the village near RAF Fairford who were evacuated due to a suspected terror plot have expressed scepticism and concern over the security response to threats made by Iran.

About 85 properties in Whelford, Gloucestershire, were evacuated on Sunday morning after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences in the village. The men, who were later re-arrested on suspicion of terror offences, were released on bail on Monday.
It is understood some residents were returning to their properties late on Monday, but a cordon remains around the village.

As speculation mounted over the circumstances surrounding the incident, concerns emerged about how events were handled by the authorities. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.

However, it remains unclear who or what was behind the alleged activity. Iran has denied any involvement. Tehran’s embassy in London condemned what it described as “unfounded and malicious speculation” linking the country to the incident in the vicinity of the military base in Gloucestershire.
Roz Savage, the MP for South Cotswolds, said she had many questions about the circumstances of how the alleged terror plot was averted.

blocks.caption: US air force personnel work on a B1 bomber at RAF Fairford on Monday. Photograph: Alastair Grant/AP

blocks.text: The Liberal Democrat MP, whose constituency covers the military base, said she would be writing to the prime minister and the defence secretary with her concerns.

“Ever since it was first announced six months ago that RAF Fairford was going to be used as the base for US military airstrikes on Iran, I’ve been asking questions of the government about whether they can assure my residents, my constituents, of their safety,” she said.
“They had given that assurance. However, I feel that the events of this weekend do cast that into doubt.”
She went on: “Who knew what? When did they know it? Where was the ball dropped? What more could have been done to secure the safety and security of my constituents?
“We are already in the process of writing to the secretary of state for defence and to the prime minister to try and ascertain the answers to some of these questions.”

There have been conflicting statements about who knew what and when. A farmer from Whelford told reporters she called police in the early hours of Sunday to report suspicious activity – which then triggered a rapid response.
But the US president, Donald Trump, also suggested to reporters the men had been under surveillance. Now, the men have been released on police bail.

Tristan Wilkinson, a cabinet member for Cotswold district council and councillor for the Lechlade, Kempsford and Fairford South ward, which covers Whelford, said: “The American president indicated last night in front of journalists that there was some intelligence and that these individuals were under surveillance.

“If that was to be true, that they would have been allowed to get so close to the base and drive what was, at the time, believed to be bombs into residential areas of a small village, I can’t imagine the security services allowing that to happen.
“I would have expected them to have done a hard stop on the van before they got to people’s homes. So that that doesn’t feel right.

“It seems insane that this appears to have been a tipoff from a member of the public, and the security services are claiming that there was a level of intelligence involved as well. I don’t see how those two things can both come through at the same time.”

He went on: “Back in July, the Iranians issued a statement saying that any countries that were providing military and practical support for the American effort were legitimate targets and at the time they named RAF Fairford specifically.
“So at that time, I and other civic leaders were calling for a more visible police presence to reassure residents, and that did happen.
“So from July, if you were around the base, you would have seen more police patrols.

“So if you’d parked a car up in a layby or somewhere near the base in the last few weeks, then you probably would have had the police contacting someone quickly to find out who you are and what you are doing.

“But I do think there’s been an increase in police presence in the last week as well. So I went past the base last Monday and I noticed that the non-manned entrances to the base have been fortified with vehicles.

“They put diggers and heavy vehicles in place that I’ve never seen before. So that’s quite an unusual step to block an emergency exit. So that led to speculation that maybe there was an increased level of concern from the base for them to use those measures.

“I wouldn’t expect the RAF to give a running commentary,” he added. “However, I think there’s always room for improvement. We have a significant military presence surrounded on three sides by residential housing. You can walk right up to the perimeter fence. There’s lots of military bases around the world that are quite remote for good reasons. So, the reality is this is a big military presence in a rural community.

“I will be asking for us to look at ways at how we can improve ongoing relations, and it’s not just relating to security matters. You know, we have other issues that you know with regard to flooding and noise, so there’s always more we can do.”

articles.title: Michael Wynn-Jones, husband of Delia Smith, dies aged 85
articles.summary:
Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday

Michael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chef Delia Smith, has died at the…

blocks.text: Michael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chef Delia Smith, has died at the age of 85.
Wynn-Jones was honorary life president of Norwich City football club, which said everyone at the club was “deeply saddened” by his death.

The club said in statement: “Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85. He will be greatly missed. His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth hospice in Ipswich.

“Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom [Smith, the couple’s nephew], and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones. At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.”
Wynn-Jones lived with Smith near Stowmarket in Suffolk and they had been married for more than 50 years.

The couple oversaw several promotions to the Premier League for the Canaries, putting the club on a solid financial footing. Smith had a more prominent, public role at Norwich City but Wynn-Jones was reportedly regarded as a trusted adviser and influential figure in the boardroom.
Darren Huckerby, a former player for the club, posted a tribute saying Wynn-Jones “stayed out of the limelight but all at Norwich City FC owe him so much”.
Wynn-Jones worked as a journalist for titles including the Daily Mirror and the Spectator and founded his own publishing company.
He began attending Norwich City games in April 1955 at the age of 13. He wrote fondly of the club’s unlikely run to the FA Cup semi-final in 1959.

Norwich City Fans Social Club said in a statement: “All of us at NCFSC are devastated to hear the news about Michael Wynn-Jones passing. Michael is a true NCFC legend and what he did for the club cannot be underestimated. We are thinking of Delia, Tom and all of Michael’s family at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Michael.”
Delia Smith previously told BBC Radio 4’s Desert Island Discs that she and Wynn-Jones bonded over their passion for food and football.
She said in 2021 she rarely cooked at home, leaving Wynn-Jones to hover over the stove while she went “to the end of the garden”.

The FBI is offering $1 million US for information leading to the arrest of a top lieutenant in the Lawrence Bishnoi gang accused of orchestrating the June 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.
Goldy Brar has' wreaked devastating havoc on countless lives,' says RCMP
The U.S. law enforcement agency is also adding Satinderjeet Singh, known as Goldy Brar, to its most wanted fugitive list.

"He joins the notorious Top 10 list because he is considered extremely violent and an enemy to the public," said Patrick Grandy, FBI assistant director in charge of the Los Angeles Field Office, during a news conference on Monday.

As part of a sweeping cross-border investigation into racketeering, extortion and murder by a trio of India-linked crime syndicates, U.S. prosecutors charged Brar in July in the killing of Nijjar. The Sikh separatist leader was shot dead three years ago by masked gunmen in the car park of the Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara.

items: Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News
'We will rule in CANADA': Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News

blocks.text: Gang leader Lawrence Bishnoi has been imprisoned since 2015, but has continued leading the gang from behind bars. Brar has been described as the North American leader of the Bishnoi enterprise and remains on the run.

"Goldy Brar and his network have wreaked devastating havoc on countless lives — through high-profile murders, shootings, death threats, extortion, arson and drug trafficking,” said RCMP Deputy Commissioner Lisa Moreland.
The FBI said Brar is considered to be extremely violent, armed and dangerous. He is known to reside in California and various parts of Canada, said Grandy.
Canada listed the Bishnoi gang as a terrorist organization in 2025, accusing it of intimidating and targeting diaspora communities.
Anyone with information about Brar is asked to contact the FBI's tip line at 1-800-225-5324.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski will represent himself at his fraud trial next week
articles.summary: Self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski’s criminal fraud and money laundering trial will begin next week, after the trial judge denied a request to delay it on Monday in Ontario's Superior Court…

image.caption: Self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski will represent himself at his criminal trial in Toronto. (Nicole Brockbank/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski’s criminal fraud and money laundering trial will begin next week, after the trial judge denied a request to delay it on Monday in Ontario's Superior Court of Justice.
Pleterski’s request to delay trial so he’d have more time to hire a lawyer was denied
Self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski's criminal fraud and money laundering trial will begin next week, after the trial judge denied a request to delay it on Monday.
Pleterski, 27, filed an application for adjournment earlier this month so he could have more time to hire a lawyer to represent him at trial.
Ontario Superior Court Justice Shaun Nakatsuru denied the request for adjournment, which means Pleterski will represent himself at his jury trial in Toronto.
"I want to assure you that even though this isn't your first choice, obviously — you will receive a fair trial," Nakatsuru said to Pleterski in court.
"I want you to be very free in asking questions … don't hesitate, just get up on your feet and ask me."

The judge also explained the "enhanced role" he will play in the trial given that Pleterski is self-represented. Nakatsuru said he will make objections on Pleterski's behalf, to ensure only admissible evidence gets in front of the jury.
Pleterski was charged with fraud over $5,000 and laundering the proceeds of crime in May 2024 by Durham Regional Police in connection with an alleged multimillion-dollar investment fraud scheme.

CBC Toronto has reported extensively on Pleterski since the summer of 2022, when he was forced into bankruptcy by some of his investors trying to recover $40 million they gave him to invest in cryptocurrency and foreign exchange.
The bankruptcy proceeding recovered about $3 million for roughly 160 investors.
Pleterski claimed family would soon help pay for lawyer
Dates for Pleterski's four-week jury trial were set in June 2025.

Pleterski hired lawyer Marco Sciarra to bring the motion for an adjournment earlier this month. In his submissions on Monday, Sciarra argued his client had been making efforts to secure the funds to retain a lawyer for trial.

If the adjournment was granted, Sciarra argued, Pleterski's extended family members were willing to liquidate assets to help him obtain a lawyer for trial. However, the names of those family members and details on the assets were not provided to the court.
Crown attorney Scott Patterson raised that issue in his submissions, and argued Pleterski has not been "honest and genuine with his attempts to obtain counsel."
Justice Nakatsuru did not provide reasons for denying the adjournment application on Monday.
The trial is set to begin next Monday, Oct. 5.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry
articles.summary: Australia is increasingly concerned about China's military might - but Beijing is also its biggest trade partner.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 2024. Relations between the two countries have been rocky in recent years
ByKaty Watson
Australia correspondent Reporting fromTownsville, North Queensland
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.
Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might.
" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan.
"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."

War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.

With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.
But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war"

blocks.text: Image source, BBC: Katy Watson
Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war"

It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight.

"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.
Binding tighter to the US

The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific.
"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.
And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.
A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing.
"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said.
"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."

The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.
But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.

The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-Pacific

blocks.text: The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-Pacific
But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US.

"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll.
"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."
The 'frenemy'
While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.
Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.
Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.
Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.
The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.

And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.
A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.
Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.
In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China is Australia's biggest export market

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
China is Australia's biggest export market

Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary.

"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones.

This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.
Rise and fall of superpowers

Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".
Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing.

"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, US President Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese. Australians have cooled on their relationship with the US under Trump

blocks.text: Image source, PMO Australia
US President Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese. Australians have cooled on their relationship with the US under Trump

But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one.
"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.

And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act.
"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says.
"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

articles.title: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant
articles.summary:
Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland

Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three Roman Catholic children – the Quinn…

blocks.text: Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three Roman Catholic children – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time.
It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today.

Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday.

Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain.

blocks.caption: A march of members of the Orange Order is blocked by police near Drumcree church, Portadown, Northern Ireland, on Monday. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

blocks.text: Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful.

The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.

The divisions and tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland, papered over by the 1998 Good Friday agreement – when all sides were exhausted by the hate and misery of the three decades of Troubles – have been all too evident of late.

This particular dispute can be reasonably argued either way. The independent Parades Commission has ruled that the march down the Garvaghy Road is permissible. The marchers are simply taking advantage of their rights, it may be said. But is it really necessary to take this road after 28 years of the march being banned? Who is served by the provocation?
The detail of the argument is perhaps less important than the fact that it is happening, and what that says about Northern Ireland today, and what it may mean for the future.

blocks.caption: Michelle O’Neill, the Northern Ireland first minister (left), and the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, (centre) in the Garvaghy Road area on Sunday. Photograph: Peter Morrison/PA

blocks.text: On the nationalist side, there has been growing and bristling self-confidence about the prospects of a border poll on a united Ireland. This was only inflated by Donald Trump’s recent suggestion that a unified Ireland should happen sooner rather than later. “The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone,” said the first minister, Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, on Monday after appearing herself in Drumcree. “We will not be going backwards.”

The numbers gathering from the nationalist community, some of whom were bussed in from Belfast and Derry, appeared to surprise the Police Service of Northern Ireland. It was a moment of unity within an often fractured nationalist community.

Those in attendance included Colin Duffy and his brother Paul, who were both acquitted of terror charges in 2015, along with the SDLP party leader Claire Hanna, a vehement critic of those who reach for violence as an answer.

Meanwhile, for the unionists, the changed relationship with the rest of the UK brought about by the Brexit deal and changing demographics has arguably engendered a distinct lack of confidence about the future.

blocks.caption: DUP MLA Jonathan Buckley (left), the party leader, Gavin Robinson, (centre) and DUP MLA Diane Dodds at Parliament Buildings, Stormont, on Monday. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP), the largest unionist party, claimed on Monday that “standards have been shattered” by the presence of the first minister with the protesters in Drumcree.

When O’Neill and Mary Lou McDonald, the leader of Sinn Féin in the Republic of Ireland, arrived at the protest, it was to chants of “bring it down” and “fuck Stormont”, in reference to power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland, structured to make unionists and nationalists work together.
“How we can go forward when there is such a level of disdain for the simple fundamental democratic principles of society?” asked Robinson of the attempt by the first minister to block a lawful march.
It is likely that the prospect of elections for the Northern Ireland assembly next year, and the need to rally the faithful to their respective cause, is not helping to calm the rhetoric.
In Stormont, the speaker, Edwin Poots, a former leader of the DUP, condemned the first minister for her “gross discourtesy” and “contempt” in not coming to answer an urgent question about the crisis.
In this context, there is concern that even if Sinn Féin’s leaders, with the crowds’ chants ringing in their ears, do not walk out of the Northern Ireland executive, that the DUP could well do so.

blocks.caption: Members of the Orange Order near Drumcree church on Monday. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

blocks.text: After a prolonged period in which agreement on a budget for Northern Ireland’s collapsing public services has not been found with Westminster, such further fracturing risks a whole new level of instability.

The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, spoke to Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, on Monday. The possibility of mediation was discussed, Mac Cionnaith said. Speaking in the Republic, Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, called for cool heads. “No one wants to go back to the past divisions, to past trauma that we experienced at Garvaghy Road, Drumcree, in the past,” he said. “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.”

articles.title: Dengue fever outbreak prompts Florida counties to declare state of emergency
articles.summary:
CDC says 392 cases of Dengue were reported for the year so far in the state, along with different county-level data

Several Florida counties recently

blocks.text: Several Florida counties recently declared a state of local emergency in response to a spate of dengue fever infections.

Hillsborough county, Florida, officials made the declaration on 24 September as health authorities recorded 134 confirmed cases of dengue fever, which is a mosquito-borne sickness typically found in countries outside the US. Officials said that the spread of the illness poses “an immediate and widespread threat to the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents and visitors of Hillsborough county”.

Controlling the tropical disease – often referred to as breakbone fever because it can cause extreme pain – requires “immediate, aggressive, and continuous” measures such as pesticide application, public education and emergency resource planning, officials said.
Dengue cases have become more common in parts of the US. In 2023, Long Beach and Pasadena reported the first ever known locally acquired cases in California.
The spread of dengue mosquitoes outside tropical and subtropical locales has even hit England, with authorities recently announcing that Aedes aegypti had been found in east London homes.
Scientists have said that global warming is poised to intensify climate-related diseases.

Declaring a local state of emergency enables Hillsborough county – whose seat is the city of Tampa – to request “any available and necessary state, federal, and local emergency funds, grants, financial assistance, and mutual aid” in their ongoing fight against mosquitoes carrying dengue. The initial declaration was put into effect for one week, but officials can extend it.
Neighboring Pasco and Pinellas counties have also declared similar states of emergency in relation to dengue reports.

The Florida department of health said in its recent report on mosquito-transmitted viruses that there were 26 cases of international travel-linked dengue reported in the state during a six-day period beginning on 13 September. There have been a total of 212 known travel-related cases in Florida reported so far in 2026.
Over the same period, there were 38 locally contracted dengue cases reported in Florida. They were among 190 cases of locally acquired dengue across Florida, the state’s health department said.

Numbers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) differ slightly. As of Monday, the CDC noted 392 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data.
Dengue is contracted through the bite of some mosquito species, largely Aedes aegypti, as well as Aedes albopictus. Both species are present in Florida.

Symptoms show up between three days and two weeks after a bite from an infected mosquito. Among the symptoms are “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain … and bleeding. Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases,” Florida’s state health department said.

The symptoms typically span four days to one week. A rarer form of the illness called dengue hemorrhagic fever can be fatal without the administration of proper supportive care, the state health department said.

Hillsborough county authorities have expressed optimism that dengue infections might slow down in the coming weeks, with zero “mosquito test pools” testing positive recently, according to the local Bay News 9 outlet.

articles.title: Stand-up comic set for release after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan
articles.summary: Turkish comedian Deniz Göktaş has been sentenced to almost 19 months, but is set to be released due to time served.

blocks.text: An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but has ordered his release due to time served.
It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey.
A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals.

Deniz Göktaş - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent.
His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views.
Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but Göktaş insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments.
"Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation."
But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. Göktaş was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday.
During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement.
"Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court.
Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal – a fellow comedian – were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict.
"We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. "
He said Göktaş would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage.

The comic is expected to be released in the coming hours, but many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days.

articles.title: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University
articles.summary: It comes after the woman filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.

blocks.text: New York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024.
The woman filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house at the university.

"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said Monday.
Cornell University said that while it supported the case being bought before a grand jury, "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false".

The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine.
Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and was incapable of providing consent.
She said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024.

The lawsuit also contains an image purported to be from a Snapchat fraternity group chat, in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe.
Van Houten said on Monday that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from her statement to authorities did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges.
He said he reached out to Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury.
In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges.

In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Jane Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack. He noted the statement differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit.
"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday.
"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
Van Houten added that Jane Doe's lawyers had never been in touch with him to say her original statement was inaccurate or to ask him to reconsider his decision not to bring charges.
He later acknowledged "the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them".

The BBC has contacted Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. In a statement on Monday obtained by CBS, the BBC's US partner, he said: "In the days following the assault, [Jane Doe] was traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode."

Giuffra said Jane Doe never spoke to anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint, adding: "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations."
"The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognise that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them," he said.

Jane Doe also alleged in her civil lawsuit that Cornell did not protect her nor adequately punish the men involved, alleging they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays".

Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the incident and the university's handling, the suit states, adding that news of the incident quickly circulated through the school.

In November 2024, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house", saying its campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students."

Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law - which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities.
On Monday, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators.
The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell".
"None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," Cornell said.
Jeremy Saland, an attorney for one of the men named in the lawsuit, denied the allegations.

Saland acknowledged his client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat", but "did nothing else." Saland denied his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine".
The case has received national attention following Doe's lawsuit and the announcement the case would be reopened. Several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, have spoken out about it.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide., external
A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.
