articles.title: US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
articles.summary: The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.

image.caption: Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the IRGC [FILE: JUNE 2022]Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo.

Earlier in September as part of "operation economic outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and potentially lose access to the US financial system.

The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies.
For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.
Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.
For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.

The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.
For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.
Major Middle East routes canceled

Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously for safety reasons that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia have been seriously disrupted.
On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.

Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
A passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.

As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.
Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.

The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.
More travelers use land crossings
With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.
One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.
"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.

For families, elderly passengers, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.
Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.
That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.
Iran's shaky aviation industry
Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions.
Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.
An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.
When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.

Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.

"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.

"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.
Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days
Iran isolated by air and sea
Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.
Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.
If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.

The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult.
If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states.
Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?

articles.title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
articles.summary: Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment".

blocks.text: Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners.

The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area.
The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners.
The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres.

With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction.

However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities.

The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it.
According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external.

In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation".
"During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said.
It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development.
The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres.
The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy.

In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community".
"This is a common-sense win for our community," he said.
"This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward.
"Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind."

articles.title: COA flags ghost, incomplete school projects in Davao del Norte
articles.summary: In Talaingod, Davao del Norte, state auditors flag a ghost school building at Kamingawan Elementary School, and undelivered project inclusions at Dulyan Integrated School

blocks.text: In Talaingod, Davao del Norte, state auditors flag a ghost school building at Kamingawan Elementary School, and undelivered project inclusions at Dulyan Integrated School

MANILA, Philippines – Around P83.26 million worth of school infrastructure projects in Davao del Norte were flagged by the Commission on Audit (COA) as ghost or non-existent, as well as “abandoned and materially incomplete” even though payments were nearly completed.
In its 2025 annual audit report on the Department of Education (DepEd), COA said the infrastructure work for Kamingawan Elementary School in Talaingod town was a “ghost/non-existent project.”
“No structure was found upon inspection but paid up to 98.8%,” state auditors noted in the report released last Wednesday, September 23.
The project was for the construction of a one-storey, two-classroom school building with a solar photovoltaic (PV) system, school furniture, and rainwater collector and water system.
A similar project for Dulyan Integrated School in Talaingod was also flagged by COA.

State auditors said that while the building and the rainwater system were constructed at Dulyan Integrated School, the “solar PV energy system as well as school furniture were not delivered,” but it was already “paid up to 98.80%.”
Both school projects were covered by a contract amounting to P36.36 million under the DepEd’s Last Mile Schools Program (LMSP), according to COA.
The commission also found another problematic LMSP project at Dugayan National High School in Kapalong town.

It had a P25.61-million contract for a two-storey, six-classroom school building with a toilet, rainwater collector, school furniture, solar PV energy system, and water system. It was already paid up to 98.90%.
“Upon inspection, building construction was found to be largely incomplete and abandoned. Only the structural frame had been constructed,” state auditors said.

COA also reported that distribution transformers, multiple panel boards, and outlets “remain uninstalled and undelivered” for New Casay Integrated School in Braulio E. Dujali town and Carmen National High School in Carmen town. Roofing works at Carmen National High School were also not performed.
The flagged school electrification projects were worth P10.43 million.

Moreover, state auditors found that four classrooms at Datu Balong National High School in San Isidro town were “unrepaired but claimed as implemented and paid up to 98.18% on July 18, 2025.” The contract was worth P7.54 million.
They also said that the construction of health facilities at Gov. Dujali Elementary School in San Isidro was “largely incomplete and abandoned.” It had a price tag of P3.32 million.
COA recommended the issuance of notices of termination of all contracts for the flagged projects, and to initiate blacklisting proceedings against the erring contractors.

State auditors told the Davao del Norte Schools Division Office (SDO) to conduct a fact-finding investigation to determine the accountability of concerned officials, initiate recovery proceedings for all paid progress billings, and file appropriate administrative, criminal, and civil charges against responsible officers and private individuals.
They also told the Davao del Norte SDO to immediately conduct joint validation of completely delivered items to correct accounting records.
State auditors also flagged deficiencies in monitoring the implementation of the DepEd’s Senior High School (SHS) Voucher Program.

In particular, guidelines for the complete monitoring and validation procedures for the SHS Voucher Program in the Ilocos Region were “not consistently followed,” which undermined the reliability of monitoring results during the audit period.
According to COA, the DepEd regional office took corrective steps from August 18 to 26.

“While the measures appear responsive to the identified deficiencies, their actual implementation and impact on ensuring compliance, detecting program violations, and validating the existence and eligibility of beneficiaries remain to be established,” state auditors said in a rejoinder.

They requested the DepEd office in the Ilocos Region to submit the comprehensive results of the 100% on-site monitoring activities, including detailed documentation of validation procedures, discrepancies, and corrective actions.

The regional office was also told to use a uniform monitoring and compliance report template to “ensure consistent verification of the existence, eligibility, and completeness of records of all SHS [Voucher Program] beneficiaries, and to enhance detection of program violations, including ghost students.”
Meanwhile, there were “inadequate payment controls” in six DepEd regional offices, which “[increased] the risk of overpayment, ghost employees, and erroneous salary payments.”
The deficiencies found were in the established payroll systems, as well as preparation, processing, and payment of salaries.
The DepEd regional offices identified in the audit observations were in the National Capital Region, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and Davao Region. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Crows are being given naloxone after suspected drug overdoses in Prince George, B.C.
articles.summary: The increased toxicity of the illicit drug supply has prompted public warnings in the north-central B.C. city.

image.caption: A female crow was found unresponsive in downtown Prince George after a suspected drug overdose. After being given nasal naloxone, she recovered. (Good Caws Crow Rescue)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The increased toxicity of the illicit drug supply has prompted public warnings in the north-central B.C. city.
Increased toxicity of illicit drug supply has prompted public warnings
An animal welfare group has been administering nasal naloxone to crows that are suspected to have eaten toxic drugs left accessible outside in downtown Prince George, B.C.
The Good Caws Crow Rescue Society (GCCRS) has posted multiple videos showing their volunteers giving nasal naloxone to crows that are otherwise unresponsive.
The videos then show the crows alert and able to fly again.

Naloxone is a medication commonly used to reverse or reduce the impact of an opioid overdose in people, and Dayna Slater of GCCRS says the crows they are helping are centred in an area of town where illicit drug use is known to occur.
"It's disheartening, it's scary," she told CBC Radio West host Sarah Penton. "It's a whole bunch of factors coming together to make, like, the perfect storm."

items: More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: Slayter said they've had one or two suspected drug overdoses a year in the past, but said they've recorded more than a dozen among crows this year alone, an alarming rise.

"Their wings are spread out, their eyes are closed, their heartbeat slows right down. They're unresponsive but alive," is how she described the symptoms, adding some have a brown liquid foam coming out of their beaks.
While some of the birds have died, she said most were able to be released after recovering within 24 hours.
Dr. Kaitlyn Liukaitis of the Birchwood Veterinary Clinic has helped treat some of the crows, and said their symptoms are consistent with a toxic drug overdose.
She also said she isn't surprised using naloxone helps reverse the symptoms, as it has become a common tool used in veterinary care to treat a variety of animals.
"It's always frustrating that, as a human population, we're so damaging to the environment," she said.
Increase in drug toxicity
Cities across British Columbia have seen a rise in toxicity in the illicit drug supply, leading to multiple public warnings.
In Prince George, overdose calls have tripled at times — leading to a constant wail of sirens downtown, which is where the crows are being found.

Outreach groups say, as there is a growing political backlash to harm reduction measures like supervised consumption sites, it is becoming more difficult for people living with addiction to access prescribed alternatives to street drugs.
They advocate for safe, indoor spaces for people to access and use drugs — in part, so they aren't left outdoors.

Slayter said she is working with harm reduction groups, who have been key to identifying crows experiencing suspected overdoses, and who have also helped supply expired naloxone kits for her volunteers to use.
She said she doesn't think anyone is intentionally harming the birds but, rather, the overdoses are a symptom of larger problems.
"They live side-by-side with us. They're in our garbage, they're in our yards. They're a direct mirror of the environment that we are living in."

items: Tripling of toxic drug overdose calls contributes to spike in sirens in Prince George
Families seeking addiction treatment say 'call back tomorrow' not an acceptable response in toxic drug crisis

blocks.text: She said she suspects the crows are accessing the drugs as they are mixed in with garbage that is openly available downtown.
She said her suggestion for a solution is more covered garbage cans that would prevent crows from accessing disposed materials.
"A crow doesn't know the difference between a sandwich bag and a bag that had something in it. And it takes something the size of like a grain of sand to affect a bird," she said.

articles.title: Hungary lifts PM Peter Magyar’s immunity, clears way for probes into 2 former Orban ministers
articles.summary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar has backed the move himself. Two former ministers who served under his rival Viktor Orban now face separate corruption probes.

image.caption: Magyar, who attended parliament, has described the case against himself as a "farce"Image: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hungary's parliament on Monday lifted Prime Minister Peter Magyar's immunity from prosecution, along with that of two former ministers from Viktor Orban's government.
The votes clear the way for investigations involving Magyar and the two opposition lawmakers, who all face separate allegations.
What did the Hungarian lawmakers decide?

Parliament voted 139-0 to lift the immunity of Magyar, former Culture and Innovation Minister Balazs Hanko and former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak. Lawmakers from Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party and its conservative Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP) ally did not take part in the vote.
Magyar, whose center-right Tisza party came to power in April, had himself called on lawmakers to lift his immunity.
Prosecutors are investigating an incident in 2024 in which Magyar allegedly took a mobile phone from a man who was filming him at a Budapest nightclub and threw it into the Danube.
Hungary suspends 'Pro-Orban' public broadcasts
Magyar has described the case as a "farce" and accused prosecutors of trying to associate his case with corruption allegations against former members of Orban's government.
What are the former Orban ministers accused of?
Hanko, now a Fidesz lawmaker, is being investigated over the alleged misuse of public money from Hungary's National Cultural Fund.
Prosecutors allege that public funds were improperly used in more than 1,000 cases, causing losses of 17.3 billion forints (€44.5 million/$52.3 million). Hanko has rejected the allegations.

Sesztak, a KDNP lawmaker who served as national development minister from 2014 to 2018, faces a separate investigation concerning alleged bribes linked to contracts involving the state-owned bus company Volanbusz.
Magyar defeated Orban in April after campaigning on a pledge to investigate alleged corruption and abuses of power during Orban's 16 years in office.

articles.title: House leaders defend 5-year barangay, SK terms
articles.summary: Two House leaders on Monday asserted the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 12326, or the Act Fixing the Term of Office of Barangay Officials and Members of the Sangguniang Kabataan to Five Years.

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 7:42pm
Two House leaders on Monday asserted the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 12326, or the Act Fixing the Term of Office of Barangay Officials and Members of the Sangguniang Kabataan to Five Years.
Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal filed a petition before the Supreme Court against the said law, calling it unconstitutional.
House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez of the second district of South Cotabato contradicted Macalintal.

"No. In fact, in the Supreme Court ruling in 2025, they already recognized that Congress is the sole authority to determine the term of the barangay officials," Hernandez said in an online interview Monday.
"Congress is just exercising our delegated power, delegated power of the Constitution that we can fix the term of barangay officials," he added.
"It's constitutional," said House Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms chairperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong in a separate online interview.

"It went through the regular process of having the two chambers pass the law. Nagkaroon naman po ng deliberation diyan sa komite. Lahat naman po ng stakeholders ay inimbitahan at nagkaroon po ng discussion diyan. Hindi naman minadali," Alonto Adiong added.
The House officials also said that the law aims to fix the term of barangay and SK officials, and that the postponement of the November 2, 2026 Barangay and SK elections was only incidental.

"There is a difference between postponement and fixing the term. Ang Macalintal case na nagsasabi na bago ka mag-postpone ng eleksiyon, kailangang mayroong criteria: that the reason must be important, substantial, and compelling. In this case, dahil ito ay fixing of the term, hindi po mag-a-apply ang Macalintal case," Hernandez explained.

When asked if Congress should have enacted two separate laws, one for fixing the term of the said officials and another for the conduct of the BSKE, Hernandez replied, "Hindi puwedeng paghiwalayin kasi when you fix the term, yung pagmo-move ng date of the election is incidental to fixing of the term. So hindi ito postponement."
"Sa palagay ko naman, it's not an issue of sino ang makikinabang. The impact of the resetting of the election is just incidental to the postponing," Adiong said.
The Commission on Elections had already started preparations for the Barangay and SK elections before the law was passed.
Hernandez and Adiong said the preparations would not go to waste even though the elections have been scheduled for November 2028.
"Well, tinanong po natin ang Comelec din dyan. Meron naman pong mga paraphernalia na pwede naman po rin magamit in the 2028 elections," Adiong stated.
"Yung mga tinta ng ballpen, baka hindi na 'yan magamit. Very minimal yung in terms of cost na makakaapekto sa budget," Hernandez added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: After Gabby sold to Ramon Ang, Piki Lopez is securing the family’s crown jewels
articles.summary: Gabby Lopez' branch turned part of their inheritance into cash—and put some of it toward keeping ABS-CBN alive. Their cousin Piki Lopez is securing control over what remains below.

blocks.text: When Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, the former chairman of ABS-CBN Corp. and the grandson of the man who built the family’s broadcast empire, sold his branch’s stake in the clan’s private holding company to diversified conglomerate San Miguel Corporation chairman Ramon S. Ang in August, the story seemed obvious: after months of cousins fighting one another in court and in the business pages, an outsider had finally bought his way into the house the Lopezes built.

The reality is that Ang bought into the family’s private penthouse, Lopez Inc., a vehicle that holds prestige and voting shares, but produces no electricity, sells no condominiums, and operates no infrastructure.

The actual wealth, the real revenue, and the plants that light a fifth of the country’s homes sit three levels below. On Friday, September 25, Federico “Piki” Lopez, Gabby’s first cousin and the chairman and chief executive of First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH) since 2010, emerged from the company’s long-delayed board election with his leadership firmly intact after months of legal and corporate deadlock. FPH is the listed company that holds much of what remains of the family’s operating empire: the power plants, industrial estates, property developments and other businesses.
Whatever truce was struck at the top, and whatever Ang believes he bought there, control of the corporate chain leading to the Lopez power business remains with Piki’s side.

items: Part 1 | Debt, discipline, and daring: Inside the Lopez Group’s high-risk bets
Part 2 | The Lopezes, presidents, and the cost of dissent
Part 3 | Lopez vs Lopez: The secrecy fight behind the Razon power deals

blocks.text: To understand why the 3rd generation cousins spent months in an acrimonious standoff, follow the cash.

Over the past two decades, the family surrendered Manila Electric Co. (Meralco) to Manuel V. Pangilinan’s group, weathered the loss of ABS-CBN’s broadcast franchise in 2020, and carried heavy debt at the holding levels. What remained standing, and thriving, was FPH. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)
FPH is not merely a paper holding firm. It is the group’s cash engine, and 3 businesses account for most of it.

Energy Development Corporation (EDC) is the jewel within the jewel. With nearly 1,300 megawatts of geothermal capacity, drawn from volcanic fields in Leyte, Negros, Bicol and Mindanao, EDC has something difficult and expensive to replicate: geothermal fields, power plants, drilling and reservoir expertise built over decades, producing renewable electricity around the clock. Since the Lopez group acquired EDC from the government in 2007, FPH president Giles Puno said more than P200 billion has been invested in the geothermal business.

First Gen Corporation is the group’s primary energy platform, built over the past 3 decades from the country’s first natural gas plants into a portfolio of geothermal, hydro, wind and solar. In 2025, First Gen sold 60% of its natural gas business to Enrique Razon’s Prime Infrastructure, freeing capital for its next phase of expansion, including roughly P62 billion into two enormous pumped-storage hydro projects in Rizal and Laguna. These are giant batteries in another form: they use electricity to pump water uphill when power is plentiful, then release it to generate electricity when the grid needs it. Roughly 92% of First Gen’s asset base is now in renewables.

Alongside them sit Rockwell Land, the developer of the Makati enclave and the malls and condominium towers that carry its name, and First Philippine Industrial Park (FPIP) in Batangas, which hosts 159 locators employing more than 73,000 people. Rockwell and FPIP add property, industrial land, and recurring income to a group dominated by power.

In 2025, FPH posted record consolidated net income of P31.7 billion on revenues of P84.7 billion, although that profit included a one-time gain from First Gen’s sale of control of its natural gas business. Recurring net income attributable to FPH shareholders was P15.1 billion.
For a family facing liquidity problems several corporate floors above, FPH was no longer just another asset. It had become the economic center of gravity.

This was why the cousins’ argument over control was also an argument over cash. Who controlled the companies would influence how much money stayed inside them for the next power plant, geothermal field or property development; how much could be sent upward as dividends; and how much, eventually, could reach other parts of the family empire, including a cash-starved ABS-CBN.
Control determined who got to make those choices.

blocks.caption: What it took to save ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The September 25 stockholders meeting of First Philippine Holdings was a direct sequel to the September 14 showdown at Lopez Holdings Corporation, formerly Benpres Holdings Corporation.
To see how control flows through the group, consider its vertical architecture.

At the apex sits Lopez Inc., the private, unlisted vehicle owned by the branches of the Lopez family, where Gabby’s Crème Investment sold its 25.68% stake to Ramon Ang. One floor down is Lopez Holdings Corporation, a publicly listed firm 54.74% owned by Lopez Inc. Below that is First Philippine Holdings, 60.67% owned by Lopez Holdings. Below FPH, the structure branches into the operating businesses: First Gen and, beneath it, EDC; Rockwell Land; the industrial park; and the rest of the companies that actually run the plants and build the buildings.

Control flows downward through those levels, and so does the proxy that carries it. At the September 14 meeting of Lopez Holdings, Piki remained chairman and CEO, while his brother Jay Lopez took over as president and COO. Their sister Mercedes “Cedie” Lopez-Vargas took another board seat, strengthening the hold of the Oscar Lopez branch on the 7-member board. Piki had secured the intermediate layer of the corporate chain.

The question was whether the consolidation would carry into FPH. That meeting had been delayed for months amid the proxy dispute between Piki and the majority cousins at Lopez Inc., with the Securities and Exchange Commission eventually ordering the election to proceed subject to a preliminary injunction issued by the Mandaluyong Regional Trial Court.

blocks.caption: Piki Lopez ring-fences the Lopez Holdings board

blocks.text: When the votes were counted on September 25, Piki’s position at FPH had survived the cousins fight. Piki was re-elected chairman and chief executive, his brother Benjamin Lopez remained vice chairman, and Francis “Giles” Puno, a career executive and his long-time second-in-command, was reappointed president and COO. Piki also kept the chair of both the executive committee and the finance and investment committee, two committees central to executive decisions and the allocation of capital.
The composition of the new 15-member board of FPH showed the controlling shareholder’s reach.

Roberta “Berta” Feliciano, a veteran director and a cousin from Gabby’s side of the family, had resigned in August, her disclosure stating plainly that her departure followed Crème Investment’s sale of its Lopez Inc. shares to Ang.

Then came the meeting itself. Shareholders elected Lee Benjamin Z. Lerma, a corporate lawyer and partner at Romulo Mabanta Buenaventura Sayoc & De los Angeles, one of the country’s older law firms, to the board. Lerma was not a returning FPH director. He was one of 5 new names nominated to the board this year.
Minutes later, Lerma was gone.

At the organizational meeting that followed the stockholders vote, Lerma resigned. According to FPH’s disclosure, he tendered his resignation “as decided by and agreed with the company’s major stockholder.” Its controlling shareholder is Lopez Holdings, which owns 60.67% of FPH and whose proxy decides the outcome of any FPH election. The board filled the vacancy the same afternoon with Victor Emmanuel B. Santos Jr., an executive vice president of the company, whose name had not appeared among the candidates shareholders were asked to elect.
The dispute did not start over green ideology. It started over cash.

After ABS-CBN’s free-television operations shut down, the media company faced mounting losses and urgent debts, and needed billions in additional capital. The holding companies above it, Lopez Inc. and Lopez Holdings, depended on dividends flowing up to meet their own obligations.

The money was being generated at FPH. Much less of it traveled all the way up the corporate pyramid. The company routed a steady P567 million a year in dividends up to Lopez Holdings, the same figure in each of the past 3 years. Lopez Holdings, after its own overhead and creditors, declared its regular 10-centavo-per-share dividend, distributing roughly P452 million. Because Lopez Holdings is publicly listed, that money goes proportionally to all its shareholders. Lopez Inc., with 54.74%, therefore received only about P247 million.
So, billions were being generated several corporate floors below. But only a fraction made the entire journey to the family’s private holding company.

But the billions inside FPH were not simply family money waiting to be withdrawn. FPH is a publicly listed company whose shareholders include the Social Security System, which owns 6.62% and invests retirement contributions of ordinary Filipinos, alongside thousands of other shareholders. Its directors owe duties to the corporation and its shareholders as a whole, not simply to the Lopez family several corporate floors above.

Gabby’s side found another way to raise cash. It converted part of its Lopez Inc. ownership into cash, then redirected part of the proceeds toward keeping ABS-CBN alive. (READ: [Rappler’s Best] The day Gabby Lopez said, ‘We’re done’)

Days after Crème Investment sold its 25.68% stake in Lopez, Inc. to Ramon Ang, ABS-CBN announced a P6-billion rescue package. P2.2 billion would come from Gabby and the other majority cousins through Crème, Mantes and Presta. Outside investor I&C Holdings committed P3.5 billion, while Lopez Inc. would put in another P300 million.

That left a fundamental tension running through this family saga: take more cash out of the operating companies now, or leave capital inside them to build the next generation of clean energy assets. First Gen was doing the latter. Its next generation of projects included about P160 billion in geothermal redevelopment over the next 5 years, and roughly P62 billion for the Wawa and Pakil pumped-storage hydro projects.
The distinction between owning shares and controlling a company became even clearer one floor below—at First Gen.

KKR, the American private equity firm that had held roughly a fifth of First Gen for years, sold its entire stake to Angsana Finance Limited, a Cayman-registered vehicle managed by Singapore-based Gateway Partners, for about P25.8 billion, or P36 a share. The sale raised an immediate question: had Angsana bought a path into the boardroom, including the seat left vacant by the resignation of First Gen director Manolo Michael de Guzman?

Asked by Rappler at the September 25 meeting, Puno answered it directly: “Because KKR acquired its 19.9% stake in First Gen directly from the secondary market, no shareholder agreement was established with FPH,” he said. “Consequently, Angsana did not obtain any special or contractual governance rights through its purchase of KKR’s holdings, maintaining only the standard statutory rights granted to minority shareholders under the Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines.”

In plain English: Angsana bought KKR’s shares, not a separate governance agreement with the Lopezes. Its 19.9% stake gives it substantial economic and voting rights, but Puno said it came with no special contractual governance rights inherited from KKR.
P25.8 billion bought Angsana almost one-fifth of First Gen. It did not automatically buy a seat in the boardroom.
The Lopez cousins’ war did not produce a neat reconciliation. It changed who owns what at the top of the Lopez pyramid, while clarifying who controls much of what lies underneath.

Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc. to Ramon Ang, converting part of its inheritance into cash. Some of that liquidity went toward the P2.2 billion that Gabby and the other majority cousins committed to keeping ABS-CBN alive. Piki, meanwhile, remained at the helm of Lopez Holdings and FPH. Farther down, FPH continues to control First Gen, which controls EDC.
One side monetized part of its inheritance. The other kept control of the operating businesses below.

The legal fight is not entirely over: Piki’s contempt petition against 4 Lopez Holdings directors remains pending before a Mandaluyong court. But when he addressed FPH shareholders on Friday, Piki did not mention the family feud.
Instead, he talked about inheritance. “Each generation inherits the results of choices made before it,” he said. “Each generation’s choices determine what it leaves behind.”

The 3rd generation Lopez cousins has spent much of 2026 fighting over that inheritance: who could speak for the family companies, who could nominate their directors, how their shares would be voted, how much cash should move upward, and ultimately who would decide what happened to the businesses previous generations had built.
Gabby’s branch turned part of that inheritance into cash—and put some of it toward keeping ABS-CBN alive. Piki Lopez is securing control over what remains below. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Carlo Paalam saves PH’s boxing campaign in Asian Games, earns sure medal
articles.summary: Carlo Paalam edges his Chinese foe as he advances to the semifinals of the men's 55kg division, preserving the Philippines' medal streak in Asian Games boxing

blocks.text: CELEBRATION. Boxer Carlo Paalam in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Carlo Paalam edges his Chinese foe as he advances to the semifinals of the men's 55kg division, preserving the Philippines' medal streak in Asian Games boxing
MANILA, Philippines – Carlo Paalam prevented what would have been a dubious first for Philippine boxing in the Asian Games.

Paalam assured himself of a medal after earning his place in the semifinals of the men’s 55kg division with a 3-2 win over China’s Zhang Jiamao at the Nishio Gymnasium in Japan on Monday, September 28.
The Olympic silver medalist won by scores of 29-28, 29-28, 29-28, 28-29, 27-30 as he preserved the Philippines’ medal streak in Asian Games boxing.

A loss by Paalam would have marked the first time the Philippines failed to win a boxing medal in the Asian Games since the sport made its debut in the 1954 edition as fellow Olympic silver medalist Nesthy Petecio earlier crashed out in the quarterfinals.
But Paalam rose to the occasion, earning the nod of three of the five judges in the opening round before delivering a more convincing second-round showing that practically sealed his victory.
Even as Zhang unanimously won the third round, he failed to erase the lead Paalam built.
With the victory, Paalam has matched his bronze finish in the 2018 edition in Jakarta, Indonesia, where he competed in the men’s 49kg category.
It does not get easier, though, for the pride of Cagayan de Oro City as he battles reigning world champion Makhmud Sabyrkhan of Kazakhstan in the semifinals on Wednesday, September 30.
Earlier on Monday, Petecio fell short of a breakthrough Asian Games medal as she suffered a 5-0 defeat at the hands of China’s Yang Chengyu in the women’s 60kg class.
Yang controlled the bout from start to finish, earning 30-26 scores from all five judges.

Other Filipino boxers have also bowed out of contention, with Junmilardo Ogayre (men’s 60kg) losing in the quarterfinals, Riza Pasuit (women’s 54kg) and Norlan Petecio (men’s 70kg) exiting the round of 16, and Aira Villegas (women’s 51kg) getting the boot in the round of 32.

Eumir Marcial, a silver medalist in the 2023 edition, was supposed to see action in this Asian Games but sat out after a mutual decision with the Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Comelec: 74M voters expected in 2028 polls
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Monday said 74 million registered voters are expected to be able to cast their ballots in the 2028 National and Local Elections.

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 7:36pm
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Monday said 74 million registered voters are expected to be able to cast their ballots in the 2028 National and Local Elections.

“We are projecting an additional three million voters. Kung sakasakali po pagdating po ng 2028, meron po tayong 74 million [voters],” Comelec chairperson George Garcia said during the agency’s Senate budget hearing.
(We are projecting an additional three million voters. If ever, by 2028, we are expected to have 74 million voters.)
He added that by November 2028, an additional one million voters are expected to vote for the 2028 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).
Comelec is seeking a P44.7-billion budget for 2027, which was reduced by 34% to P29.5 billion.
The poll body is currently drafting the terms of reference for the voting machines to be used for the 2028 NLE as it plans to procure new units.
Last week, President Ferdinand Marcos signed into law a bill that postponed the BSKE to 2028 and extending the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials from four to five years.
With this move, Garcia said the poll body will open voter registration by the second week of November this year, until June 30, 2028.

“Pag nag-reset tayo ng BSKE, lagi po kaming hihingi ng dagdag na budget. Kasi po dagdag na botante, dagdag na presinto, dagdag na electoral board members, dagdag na election paraphernalia,” Garcia said.
(If we reset the BSKE, we will always need to request additional funding because more voters mean more polling precincts, more electoral board members, and more election paraphernalia.)
The poll body had said that it already spent P8 billion of its P19-billion budget for the BSKE, adding that some election supplies, including indelible ink, may go unused if the BSKE is postponed.
Comelec is hoping that Congress would allow them to use the BSKE budget for the NLE.
“Maibabalik po namin yung P9.2 billion na nawala kay Comelec para sa national and local elections,” Garcia said.
(We can restore the P9.2 billion that was taken away from the Comelec’s budget for the national and local elections.)
TRO vs BSKE postponement

Earlier today, election lawyer Romulo Macalintal filed a petition with the Supreme Court (SC) seeking the issuance of a temporary restraining order TRO against the postponement of the BSKE in November 2026.

In his petition, Macalintal asked the Court to issue a TRO or a status quo ante order directing the Office of the President, through the Executive Secretary, the Senate, the House of Representatives, and the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to refrain from implementing Republic Act (RA) No. 12326.
Aside from this, he asked the SC to declare the law inoperative, invalid, and/or unconstitutional in so far as it pertains to the postponement of the BSKE.
Should the BSKE be pushed through on November 2, Garcia said, "Mukhang hindi namin kaya ang November 2. However, the Comelec always has the power to declare the postponement of elections.”
(It looks like we won’t be able to meet the November 2 schedule. However, the Comelec always has the power to declare a postponement of elections.)
Under the Omnibus Election Code, Comelec can postpone an election if there is terrorism, violence, or force majeure.
The filing of the Certificate of Candidacy for the BSKE was initially scheduled from Sept. 28 to Oct. 5, 2026. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Israel does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advised
articles.summary: Former attorney general Dominic Grieve says Israel is not entitled to shut mission in occupied Palestinian territory

blocks.text: Israel does not have a legal right to act on its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the former attorney general Dominic Grieve has advised the UK Foreign Office.
Israel has said it intends to shut the consulate on 8 October in response to the sweeping ban on trade with goods from Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, this month.

Israel said on Sunday that it planned to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements.

Grieve, who was a Conservative MP between 1997 and 2019 and attorney general from 2010 to 2014, said Israel did not have the right to shut the consulate since it was situated in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.

When challenged in the Lords by the former UK ambassador Lord Hannay on the legality of Israel’s action, the Foreign Office minister Lord Wood said his fellow peer may have a point, and knew more about the subject than he did, but that he feared Israel de facto could make the consulate inoperable.
Grieve said the UK should challenge the decision in the courts, arguing Israel was asserting a right it did not possess as an occupying power to impose sovereign control over East Jerusalem.

blocks.caption: Dominic Grieve, who was attorney general under David Cameron. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

blocks.text: The UK mission in Jerusalem dates from 1838, predating the creation of the state of Israel by more than 100 years, and is separate from the embassy based in Tel Aviv. The consul general reports direct to the Foreign Office, and has its own staff and a distinct diplomatic role, covering Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza.

Grieve argues in an advisory paper sent to the Foreign Office by the British Palestine Project that “retaining a consulate general in East Jerusalem after recognition of the state of Palestine preserves the UK’s position that Jerusalem’s final status remains to be determined. It does not concede Israeli sovereignty.”

Grieve said the UK government had a duty to oppose the move. He pointed out the UK government had formally accepted the July 2024 advisory opinion of the international court of justice that governments should recognise Israel’s presence in occupied Palestinian territory as unlawful.

Separate from the legal position, Grieve said the closure of the consulate was a measure designed to fall on Palestinians, not on Britain alone, because it would hamper aid, oversight and reporting from the West Bank and Gaza.

He said: “Israel’s method in the city has been to create facts on the ground through unlawful settlement building and property seizure, and to press states to recognise those facts diplomatically. The closure should be challenged as a further attempt to exercise powers outwith those permitted to an occupier.”

In closing the consulate, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, asserted Israeli sovereignty over the whole city of Jerusalem, which the UN security council has expressly said Israel does not possess.
after newsletter promotion

The decision to revoke credentials of Dutch diplomats, announced by Sa’ar on Sunday, also in effect bars them from Israeli-controlled East Jerusalem and is likely to force the closure of their representative office in Ramallah.

The Netherlands’ ban on imports from occupied Palestine came into force on 22 September. The guidance applies to companies and individual travellers, and covers items bought before or after the legislation came into force, including gifts, souvenirs and items for personal use, the Dutch customs authority said.
Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine.

Sa’ar claimed that Dutch diplomats from the Ramallah mission could continue representing their nation’s interests “from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the state of Israel”. The Israeli foreign ministry did not immediately respond to questions about how this would work in practical terms.

When Israel took the same measures against Norwegian diplomats in 2024, in response to the country’s decision to recognise Palestine, it was forced to close its mission based in the West Bank town of al-Ram.

“We consider the Netanyahu government’s decision to be extreme and unreasonable,” the Norwegian foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said at the time. Diplomats based in Jordan have supported Norwegian relations with Palestine since then.

articles.title: Sara Dutere impeachment trial: Luisto tong-its remark stricken off the record
articles.summary: The “tong-its” remark of House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro was stricken from the record of the Senate impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday after she likened three alleged…

blocks.text: The “tong-its” remark of House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro was stricken from the record of the Senate impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday after she likened three alleged violations by the Vice President to “three hits” in the popular card game.

Luistro made the remark while responding to Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo’s question on whether GenCorp Industries Inc.—an asset Duterte declared in her 2024 and 2025 statements of assets, liabilities and net worth—could bid for and secure government contracts from Davao City Hall, led by her brother, Vice Mayor Sebastian Duterte.

“If there’s SALN already, which the Vice President herself acknowledged and admitted, that she is part of this corporation, then GenCorp should not be participating in the bidding of the City of Davao, which is headed by no less than the brother of the Vice President. This is a conflict of interest contemplated under Article 7, Section 13 of the Constitution,” Luistro said, referring to the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

“The Honorable Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian is very much correct when he said that there must be disclosure of the relationship of the merchant to any of the officials of the procuring entity, Your Honor, and I totally agree with the Honorable Senator Raffy Tulfo when he implied the three violations on the part of the Vice President: owning business. Operating a business and conflict of interest, Your Honor. In fact, kung sa larong tong it, three hits po ito,” Luistro added.
She was referring to a situation in a card game tong-its wherein a player loses three consecutive times.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, however, removed Luistro’s three hits comment from the impeachment proceedings record.

Article 7 Section 13 of the Constitution reads, “The President, Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants shall not, during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries.”
The same provision adds, “They shall strictly avoid conflict of interest in the conduct of their office.”

In a separate press conference, Luistro reiterated her answer to senator-judges’ questions that, as far as the prosecution is concerned, the Vice President violated laws due to her involvement in GenCorp.

“How are you going to question the credibility of the document, especially if it is issued by government offices? This is with respect to PhilGEPS (Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System), in relation to the question of senator-judge Raffy Tulfo,” Luistro said.
PhilGEPS is the repository of government contracts.

PhilGEPS Division Chief Rendell Sopeña earlier told the Senate impeachment court that around 11 contracts worth P7 million to P8 million in total were granted by the Davao City government to GenCorp Industries under a negotiated bidding.

Sopeña also testified that various government agencies awarded around P35 million worth of contracts to GenCorp. Industries during Vice President Duterte’s term, with 49 contracts awarded to the company.
Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, for his part, said the Constitution was explicit in its prohibitions.

“The prohibition under the Constitution is direct or indirect participation in any business or financial interest. Indirect means kahit hindi derecho nakapangalan sa iyo ang shares of stock, kahit nakapangalan sa ibang tao, dahil nga indirect [ang sabi ng Constitution], ipinagbabawal ‘yan,” Tolosa said.
(Even if the shares of stock are not under your name and are under the name of other people, the Constitution covers indirect [participation], so that it is still prohibited.)
“Iyon iyong kailangan tignan dito, na [kung] meron ba siyang violation roon,” Tolosa added.
(This is what we need to take a look at here.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Mexico's Pacific coast braces for Hurricane Polo
articles.summary: The category-four storm is approaching the state of Baja California Sur, on Mexico's northern Pacific coast.

blocks.text: People living on the northern Pacific coast of Mexico are bracing for the arrival of Hurricane Polo, which is forecast to make landfall later on Monday or early on Tuesday.

The category three storm, with maximum sustained winds near 115 mph (185 km/h), is expected to move over the state Baja California Sur, a region popular with tourists and home to the resort destination of Los Cabos.
Meteorologists at the US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) have warned of heavy rainfall which could lead to life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.
Residents on Sunday stocked up on essentials such as drinking water and food as the storm approached.
The NHC warned of the storm surge Hurricane Polo could unleash, which it said could be accompanied by large and destructive waves.

In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, the authorities restricted access to the beaches. Some restaurants also closed in the town, which acts as a base for sport fishers and whale watchers.

articles.title: Mary Jane Veloso’s journey home is a story of grit
articles.summary: Mary Jane Veloso did not lose hope that she would someday be free and reunited with her family, and that homecoming has finally become reality

items: Mary Jane Veloso was granted an absolute pardon by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. after 16 years of imprisonment.
Before returning home, she attended Mass and held a press conference to express gratitude to her supporters.
Upon arriving home in Nueva Ecija, she was warmly welcomed by family and friends.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Throughout Saturday, September 26, Mary Jane Veloso rubbed liniment oil on the temples of her head. It temporarily soothed the headache she had been feeling since Friday, September 25.

It seemed her weakened body held her back from moving freely all day. But her will was stronger. Maybe because she already endured 16 long years of imprisonment that being sick for another day could not stop her from doing engagements and traveling for hours.

After all, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. already granted the 41-year-old former overseas Filipino worker (OFW) an absolute pardon from her drug trafficking conviction handed down by an Indonesian court in 2010.
All Mary Jane needed to do was to reach her doorstep in Nueva Ecija, so she could announce to the world that she was home at last.

blocks.caption: NEW MORNING. Cesar and Celia Veloso hold onto their daughter Mary Jane as they leave a hotel in Manila on September 26, 2026, after spending the night following the former overseas Filipino worker’s release from the Correctional Institution for Women. Photo by Rappler

blocks.text: Mary Jane did not go home immediately after leaving the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City early Saturday.

She and her family spent the night in Manila, as she wanted to attend Mass first and hold a press conference before going back to her home province. It was her way of giving back to supporters and all other Filipinos who followed her case.
Overwhelmed by her reunion with her family, Mary Jane could not sleep.

During the ride to Siena College Chapel in Quezon City, sleepless Mary Jane took time to appreciate the world outside of prison in broad daylight, specifically the roads, as well as the trees and plants, her 46-year-old sister Maritess Laurente told Rappler.

The medicine they gave to Mary Jane did little to ease her motion sickness. Nuns gave her warm water and crackers. Afterwards, she wore her rosary then rested her head on the shoulders of her father, 70-year-old Cesar, as they waited for the Mass to start.

blocks.caption: Mary Jane Veloso’s journey home is a story of grit

blocks.text: The former OFW was fueled by her faith. Recalling the moments before her scheduled execution in Indonesia in April 2015, she told journalists: “Sabi ko kay God, ‘Patunayan mo sa buong mundo na wala akong kasalanan. Iligtas mo po ako.’” (I asked God, “Prove to the world that I’m innocent. Please save me.”)
She was granted a last-minute reprieve in Indonesia. Over a decade later, she was pardoned in the Philippines.

“Natutunan ko po talaga sa laban ko na ‘to na huwag tayong bibitaw. Huwag tayong mawalan ng pag-asa kasi ibibigay ni God ‘yan sa tamang panahon. At ito po ‘yong panahon na iniintay ko, dumating na po: Kasama ko ang aking pamilya.”

(What I learned from my fight for freedom is we should not let go. We should not lose hope because God will grant our desires at the right time. And the moment that I’ve been waiting for has arrived: I’m with my family.)

blocks.caption: THANKSGIVING MASS. Mary Jane Veloso, accompanied by her family and support groups, attends a thanksgiving Mass at Siena College Chapel in Quezon City on September 26, 2026. Photo by Jire Carreon/Rappler

blocks.text: The Veloso family also could not sleep after the release of Mary Jane, the youngest of five children of Cesar and Celia. Her siblings thought what was happening was a dream.

Christopher Veloso, 48, was working on their farm when he heard that his sister had been pardoned. With their eagerness to be reunited with her, they forgot to bring clothes for Mary Jane. It was supporters from rights group Migrante International who lent Mary Jane a pink top, which she wore during Saturday’s press conference.

When they settled at a hotel in Manila in the early hours of Saturday, they ordered pizza. Even with their separate hotel rooms, 14 members of the Veloso family crowded in one room to share the midnight snack and be with Mary Jane.
They wanted to make up for lost time with Mary Jane, the most affectionate Veloso, after her 16-year ordeal behind bars.
Darling Cando, 44, who was described as the sibling closest to Mary Jane, massaged her sister’s aching head.
Mary Jane clung to her mother when she faced the media after Saturday’s Mass. Celia, 66, would touch and fix her youngest daughter’s hair from time to time.

blocks.caption: MOTHER’S LOVE. Mary Jane Veloso and her mother Celia join a press conference at Siena College in Quezon City on September 26, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Sa nakita ko sa kapatid ko, kahit gano’n ang nangyari sa kanya, talagang nilakasan niya ang loob niya,” Christopher told Rappler.
“Kung tatanungin ako kung ‘yong ginawa niya, nakulong siya nang matagal, kung kakayanin ko, baka ‘di ko kaya eh. Kaya bilib ako sa kanya. Salamat po at ginabayan siya ng Panginoon.”

(From what I’ve seen from my sister, she really remained strong even if she was imprisoned for a long time. If I were in her shoes, I think I wouldn’t be able to handle that. That’s why I’m proud of her. Thank you, Lord, for guiding her.)
With Mary Jane’s freedom, her siblings said they will strive to keep their promises, such as attending Mass every week and helping her start a business.

blocks.caption: Mary Jane Veloso’s journey home is a story of grit

blocks.text: And for Mary Jane, she can now fulfill her desire to take care of her aging parents and her own sons, Mark Daniel Candelaria, 23, and Mark Darren Candelaria, 17.

Daniel and Darren were only seven years old and one year old, respectively, when their mother left the Philippines to be a domestic worker in April 2010. She was supposed to take a job in Malaysia, but was asked by her recruiters to go to Indonesia instead with a new suitcase. In Indonesia, airport authorities found heroin hidden inside the lining of Mary Jane’s bag. She was arrested for drug trafficking and later placed on death row.

Maintaining her innocence, Mary Jane would spend the next 16 years fighting for her freedom. Her life was spared in 2015 due to the last-minute reprieve, and in December 2024, she again stepped on home soil as Indonesia agreed to transfer her to Philippine custody.

Now, Mary Jane will finally be with her sons on their birthdays — with Darren turning 18 on October 25 and Daniel turning 24 on November 28. Her sons, now young men, cried during Saturday’s press conference when their mother spoke, when she recited poetry, and when she sang “Maghintay Ka Lamang.”

Daniel and Darren also delivered heartfelt messages to the mother they grew up without, yet love so dearly. “Tandaan ‘nyo po palagi na proud na proud po ako na kayo po ‘yung naging nanay ko,” Daniel said. (Always remember that I’m so proud you’re my mother.)

blocks.caption: Mary Jane Veloso’s journey home is a story of grit

blocks.text: After more than two hours of travel, Mary Jane arrived in General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija, at 5:43 pm on Saturday. Relatives and some neighbors greeted Mary Jane, who was still carsick but clearly thrilled to be home.

blocks.caption: HOMECOMING. Mary Jane Veloso waves to supporters upon her arrival in General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija, on September 26, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: Carefully, she walked towards their house, where banners and balloons were put up to mark her homecoming. This was her first time to see their house in General Mamerto Natividad, as their family is originally from Talavera, another town in Nueva Ecija.
She was given warm water to drink before she changed into a more comfortable black shirt.
For her first meal back home, Mary Jane requested pinakbet — a Filipino vegetable dish — and grilled fish. The General Mamerto Natividad government also gave a chocolate cake.

blocks.caption: Mary Jane Veloso’s journey home is a story of grit

blocks.text: “Puro repolyo naman. Mahal po kasi ang gulay, pasensiya na (It’s full of cabbage. Vegetables now are expensive, please bear with us),” Christopher said of the pinakbet, which was prepared by his wife, Nerisa. Chuckles were heard around the table as the Veloso family gathered to eat.
As the night wore on, neighbors started a karaoke fest. Mary Jane inched closer to her relatives and friends, chatting about her imprisonment.

blocks.caption: ‘KUMUSTAHAN.’ Mary Jane Veloso spends the night chatting with family and friends back home in Nueva Ecija on September 26, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: Color returned to Mary Jane’s face. “Nakakain na eh (I’ve already eaten, that’s why),” she told Rappler.
But perhaps it was because she was home at last. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
articles.summary: Deniz Goktas was convicted of two of three charges, including "insulting" the president, but was released pending the appeal process. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.

image.caption: Goktas' show 'Dead Sea' gathered traction online in July, and shortly thereafer the comedian was detained on arrival at Istanbul's airport [Undated photo from the show]Image: YouTube/Deniz Göktaş

blocks.text: A Turkish comedian was convicted in Istanbul on Monday on charges of "insulting" President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and "insulting religious values" during a stand-up performance in June.
The judge provisionally sentenced Deniz Goktas to 19 months in prison, but ordered his release pending the judicial review and appeal process that would finalized the verdict.
It was not immediately clear how long this process might take.
NATO member and EU aspirant Turkey routinely tries people on speech-related offenses, particularly and famously when it comes to supposed "insults" of its longserving leader Erdogan.
What was the case about?

Deniz Goktas, 32, was arrested on July 3, a week after releasing a YouTube video of his show that was watched nearly 9 million times and a few days after shorter clips he posted on X enjoyed similar rapid success.
He faced an array of charges related to content in his "Dead Sea" show. Goktas referred to his impending court appointment online on Sunday, in one of his irreverent social media posts from his cell.

Goktas was accused of insulting Erdogan, of inciting public hatred and hostility — via jokes about Islam — and of praising crime and criminals, an additional charge added by prosecutors tied to a joke about an organized crime family, the Daltons

His trial is the latest in a widening crackdown on people seen as critical of Turkey's moderate Islamist government. Hundreds of politicians, artists, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists are among those to face detenion or trial.
LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown
What did Goktas say in his defense in court?
Goktas did not dispute the content from his popular show, but did argue in court that he had committed no crimes with his jokes.
Prosecutors had for instance singled out a pair of references he made to President Erdogan as a "dictator" as illegal insults.

"Dictator is not an insult: it is a political characterization," Goktas told the court. "As the president and leader of the party that has ruled the country for 25 years, a political comedy show in which Erdogan's name is never mentioned would be neither sincere nor have any connection to reality."
He said that Erdogan should be "open to the art of satire," as he said past presidents in Turkish democracy were.
"The joke hasn't changed. What has changed is the increasingly fragile leadership that can no longer tolerate the joke," he said.

The judge nevertheless convicted Gotkas of insulting Erdogan, and downgraded the charge he faced of "inciting hatred and hostility" with jokes about Islam, instead convicting him of the lesser supposed crime of "insulting religious values."
He cleared the comedian of the third charge of allegedly praising criminality.
Goktas has spent just under three months in pretrial detention, which should count as time served in any potential custodial sentence.

blocks.caption: News of Goktas' arrest in early July prompted protest in Istanbul [FILE: July 3, 2026]Image: Yasin Akgul/AFP

blocks.text: Erdogan the only claimant, Diyanet religious authority among those to complain
According to the Turkish NGO the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA), prosecutors cited more than 500 applications to prosecute the performer regarding the show.

They were issued to the Presidential Communication Center that monitors such issues. One of the groups to provide a tipoff was the government-sponsored Presidency of Religious affairs, better known as Diyanet.
Erdogan, in charge of Turkey either as prime minister or later president since 2003, was named as the sole complainant.

His government has attracted attention in recent years for its prosecution of people deemed to have unfairly criticized the authorities, and for the various lawsuits against leading members of the opposition, particularly the CHP. The Turkish president's litigious streak also became headline news in Germany around a decade ago, when he pursued star TV comedian Jan Böhmermann.

Meanwhile the MLSA said that Goktas' jokes alleged to have the potential to "publicly incite hatred and hostility" took aim at fundamentalist Islam, including a reference to women in full-coverage swimsuits being "divers" and joking about "suicide bombers who fast."
Turkey nominally has a secular constitution and guarantees of free speech. However, the EU and the US have often criticized its application of these standards.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom wrote in a 2022 report that Erdogan's government increasingly relied on speech-based prosecution to "silence individuals who express criticism in religious terms, disclose beliefs or a lack thereof that differ from those of the majority of the population, or engage with religion in a way perceived as 'mocking' or 'irreverent.'"
