articles.title: Can I get AI face? Plastic surgeons say AI-generated inspiration is more than meets the eye
articles.summary: Some plastic surgeons in Canada and elsewhere say they're seeing more people coming in for consultations with AI-modified images of themselves, seeking cosmetic procedures that work that will mirror…

blocks.text: Plastic surgery patients are looking for 'AI face'
Dr. Ian MacArthur is accustomed to dealing with new trends in cosmetic surgery, but he's starting to see more patients coming into his Ottawa clinic with expectations that aren't entirely realistic.
Some clients, he says, bring in "fairly stylized" images generated with artificial intelligence, seeking results that may not even be "physically possible."
The experiences he's had so far motivated him to share a few cautionary thoughts on his Instagram page.
But it's a trend that plastic surgeons are dealing with more often.

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS) recently warned about the rise of "AI face" — flawless, AI-enhanced images of patients' own faces that they believe can be recreated surgically.
The concern, says the organization's president, is that AI could also lead some people to put their desire for an unachievable look ahead of their own safety and well-being.
"The less realistic the image, the more dangerous that becomes if someone says, 'Yes, I can do it,'" Dr. Nora Nugent told CBC News.
More than meets the AI

BAAPS surveyed about half its roughly 350 members about how often they're seeing instances of AI face during consultations, Nugent said, with about 15 per cent of them responding that it's happening more often.

It's not that people are asking for anything unusual, she says. It's that the chatbot may have made other enhancements that it doesn't immediately disclose, such as a sharpened jawline or smoothed-out skin.

items: Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down

blocks.text: CBC News uploaded a photo of a journalist's face to three commonly used generative AI platforms — the free versions of OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google Gemini's Nano Banana and Anthropic's Claude — and prompted them to show the outcome of a rhytidectomy (a facelift).
Claude would not complete the task, responding that it wouldn't generate "realistic manipulated images of actual people."

Nano Banana did complete the task. When prompted, the chatbot explained that in addition to simulating the rhytidectomy, it also reduced loose neck skin and applied dermatological treatments like laser resurfacing or a chemical peel. (It also appeared to shave off facial hair).
It would not, however, create a medical before-and-after image comparison, encouraging consulting with a certified plastic surgeon for a realistic assessment.

ChatGPT did not hesitate to produce a visualization, as well as a side-by-side comparison. Like Nano Banana, it actually simulated multiple procedures — including what appeared to be an eyelid lift, brow lift and neck lift. ChatGPT said it smoothed out the forehead.
The chatbot did not immediately recommend consulting with a surgeon but later said the outcomes depend on one's anatomy, goals and doctor.
Pixels, not human tissue
Nugent says it's important for anyone seeking cosmetic surgery to know that AI can't account for an individual's anatomy.
"[AI] works in pixels, not human tissue," she said.

"Some tissue intrinsically is stronger, has more collagen, maybe thicker skin, and will hold a lift better," she said, adding that there are limits to "what's structurally safe to do" with a person's face.

items: New Brunswick is weaving AI into its K-12 curriculum, drawing praise — and pushback
Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?

blocks.text: "If you make a nose too small and too narrow, that person won't be able to breathe properly through their nose," she said. "If you take too much skin from an eyelid, someone can't close their eyes properly and that creates a medical problem."
On top of that, a patient's age, weight and lifestyle are also factors in the outcome.
AI deepfakes of prominent Canadian doctors are coming for your money
Nugent says people can likely recognize the "more extreme changes" as unrealistic.
"But it's the mild to middle changes that they might think are realistic," she said.

Karen Rowa, a psychiatry and behavioural neurosciences professor at Hamilton's McMaster University, says it could also worsen problems for those who struggle with their appearance or have body dysmorphic disorder.

AI chatbots tend to "please the person they're talking to," she says. Asking them to fix something a person doesn't like about their face or body may "reinforce a problem that may not actually exist."
An unachievable risk
Dr. Michael Weinberg says he hasn't consulted any patients who have used generative AI tools to simulate their cosmetic surgery outcomes, but he's not entirely against the idea.

Weinberg, a plastic surgery division lead at Ontario's Trillium Health Partners, says AI may help a patient visualize their own goals in advance of an appointment. A surgeon can then help them determine what's possible and what's not.
He says plastic surgeons have already been using digital 3D simulation tools in their consultations for some time — for procedures like breast augmentations or eyelid lifts.
"If it's used wisely and judiciously with realistic results, then it is great because it can show you what you can look like," he said.

items: Paging Dr. AI to the ER? Artificial intelligence shows promise in emergency room diagnosis

blocks.text: What he worries about is doctors who overpromise on what can be achieved — whether it's due to inexperience, pressure from the patient or unscrupulous business practices.

"There's a lot of bad plastic surgeons," he said, and a patient's desire to meet AI-generated expectations may lead them to seek less reliable options if they're told that their goals aren't achievable by a more responsible doctor.
He says "tourist plastic surgery" is another issue, with some people travelling abroad for aesthetic procedures.
That comes with a big risk, Weinberg says, of returning with the "absolute worst complications" that can require additional surgeries and months of care.
LISTEN | Just how dangerous is AI — and what we should do about it:
Front Burner33:35Why are AI leaders calling for a slow down?

But Ottawa surgeon MacArthur says most patients are reasonable and aren't looking to go to any extremes. He says those who turn to AI tools may be doing so because they want to better communicate their wishes.

As long as he's clear with them about what is achievable, he says, they're generally understanding. But he does think some people have unrealistic expectations, and that AI could "be like gasoline on the fire."

articles.title: 'Thrown under the bus': Former defence chief's memoir lays bare his battles with the Trudeau government
articles.summary: Former defence chief Wayne Eyre considered quitting "several times" as he battled the Trudeau government over military misconduct, defence spending and support for Ukraine. His candid memoir recounts…

image.caption: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau shakes hands with Gen. Wayne Eyre, outgoing Chief of the Defence Staff, after his remarks at a change of command ceremony in Ottawa on July 18, 2024. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada's former top military commander considered resigning "several times" during his tenure in battles with the former Trudeau government over the sexual misconduct scandal, and the lack of commitment towards defence spending.

Retired general Wayne Eyre's new memoir, Into the Breach: A Soldier's Journey, also peels back the curtain on the internal debate that took place over how to end the convoy occupation of downtown Ottawa in early 2022.
The prologue to the book, titled The Accidental CDS, is a tongue-in-cheek reference to his unusual, unexpected rise to the position of chief of the defence staff.

Eyre was promoted from being army commander to the top job after now-retired admiral Art MacDonald stepped aside in February 2021 because of allegations of inappropriate behaviour. Those allegations never resulted in charges and MacDonald didn't return to the defence chief's job.
Eyre was left to navigate the wider sexual misconduct scandal and a flurry of allegations which engulfed several high-ranking military leaders — an experience he described as "soul crushing."
He candidly writes about how, in the first few months, he often questioned whether he was up to the task.
Eyre's memoir recounts a highly charged incident in June 2021 where he said he felt thrown "under the bus" by former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland.

At the time, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Freeland both publicly questioned Eyre's decision to allow the now-former commander of the navy, Vice-Admiral Craig Baines, to remain in his post after he took part in a golf game with former chief of the defence staff Jonathan Vance, who had been under military police investigation following allegations of inappropriate behaviour.
In Eyre's view, Freeland's criticism amounted to forcing the prime minister to choose between his deputy and his senior military adviser.

"If there's no trust between the nation's senior military leader and the nation's senior elected leader, one of them has to go, and it's not going to be the elected leader," Eyre said in an interview with CBC News.
Support from Trudeau kept him from resigning

The incident culminated, Eyre said, when he was on the phone with the prime minister to discuss the decision to retain Baines. He was just about to resign when Trudeau stopped him by saying he still had confidence in him.

After his initial criticism, the prime minister made a further statement of support for his defence chief — remarks Eyre had not seen when the phone call was placed. The crisis was defused, but the tension remained.
Former military commander Eyre says he thought about resigning 'several times'
Eyre served another three years after the incident.
Resignation crossed his mind "several times" as internal battles unfolded over defence funding and the deteriorating state of readiness in the military.
Ultimately, he decided to stay because quitting would have precipitated a further crisis in an already wounded institution.
"You've got to be very careful as a military leader about resigning. You can fall on your sword, but generally it hurts and you can only do it once," he said.

"Resigning is an inherently political act, which could further fray political-military relations, [and] would cause a momentary blip in the media cycle. But at the same time, [it would] cause significant turmoil in the institution."

items: Gen. Wayne Eyre stepping down from position as Canada's top military commander

blocks.text: Throughout his tenure there was a series of rolling crises including the various waves of the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 11, 2022.
At the time, the Trudeau government faced public criticism about its reluctance to approve lethal aid for the embattled Eastern European country. It was a struggle, Eyre acknowledged.
"What we experienced at that time was a collision of ideology with reality," he told CBC.
"The ideology being, we are Canada, we don't supply weapons to a conflict zone. The reality was, OK, this is coming, Ukraine is a friend, this [is] one way we can help."
'Lethargy to approve a new defence policy'

Eyre's book is littered with further examples related to Canada's mission to train Ukraine troops and the transfer of M-777 artillery, underlining his frustration with the government's seeming "inability to make decisions at the speed of war."
He did note there were times when Canada later outstripped its allies in the swift delivery of war supplies and equipment, such as Leopard tanks.
The overall sense of frustration came into sharp focus during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's September 2023 visit to Canada, which included a series of speeches in Toronto.

items: Zelenskyy's 1st visit to Canada since Russia's war 'emotional,' say some Ukrainians

blocks.text: "Both the PM and Deputy PM Freeland gave bellicose, impassioned speeches about being strong and supporting Ukraine," Eyre wrote, noting the contradiction between the political rhetoric and the fiscal reality that faced the Canadian military at the time.

"I, like the handful of CAF senior leaders present, had a hard time reconciling these otherwise great speeches with both the billion-dollar budget cut that they had just inflicted on us and their lethargy to approve a new defence policy."
The deeper the war in Ukraine became, the more concerned Eyre became about the state of Canada's readiness.
‘Urgency is required,’ says outgoing chief of defence staff Gen. Wayne Eyre on Russia-Ukraine war

He described how, in June 2022, during the run-up to the unveiling of Canada's new policy commitment to NORAD — the by national aerospace command — no one seemed to know where $38 billion in funding was going to come from, or where it would be allocated.

"Most galling was the 'smoke and mirrors' funding approach, with billions already allocated for other military equipment taken away and reallocated, with most investments only coming years into the future," Eyre wrote.
"With confusion persisting several days later, I drew some government ire when I frankly told a journalist that the source of funds 'wasn’t clear to me.'"

items: Top soldier says military looking for 'clarity' on Ottawa's budget plans

blocks.text: Military 'compartmentalized' Ottawa convoy involvement
The memoir also sheds light on a passing reference that appeared in the public hearings related to the invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the convoy protest.

Former deputy defence minister Bill Matthews testified that the military prepared operational plans as a precaution, but they were dismissed due to significant concerns that deploying troops would escalate tensions and mirror the 1990 Oka Crisis.

Throughout the convoy protest crisis, Eyre was firmly opposed to the notion that the military had any sort of role whatsoever. He attempted to correct the public perception by saying there's a difference between planning and scenario spinning.
"We looked at various scenarios, and it wasn't planning because a plan entails assigning troops to task and warning at all levels and the like," Eyre told CBC News.

"No, it was more thinking about various scenarios, and what questions would we have to ask, what measures would have to be taken. But given the sensitivity at the time, it was very compartmentalized."
Most of the discussion, he said, revolved around the use of military tow-trucks to remove protest vehicles.
In his memoir, Eyre wrote: "At the time one of my staff commented, 'If you accomplish nothing else as CDS, keeping the CAF out of this mess is a singular achievement.'"
Canada 'on the right path,' Eyre says
During his final months as defence chief and in his departure speech, Eyre warned about how dangerous the world had become and how Canada needed to prepare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government reversed many Trudeau-era policies and has begun substantially investing in defence — taking the country to the NATO standard of two per cent of the gross domestic product.

Several European political leaders, as well as security and intelligence agencies have warned that the West is likely to face a major conflict with Russia and possibly even China by the end of the decade.
Asked by CBC whether he thought the country was ready for what may be coming in the next few years, Eyre said no.
"But we're on the right path, and we are getting there."

articles.title: Trump's tariffs are unpopular in Maine. A Republican senator may pay the price
articles.summary: The Canada-U.S. trade war is playing out amid a tight race for U.S. Senate in Maine. The election result will help determine which party controls Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump's term as…

image.caption: U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, centre, walks with her supporters in a parade in the town of Carmel, Maine. Collins is seeking a sixth term on Nov. 3 and the Republican is running on a platform that includes opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

blocks.text: If U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs could bring manufacturing back to places it has fled, the town of Millinocket, Maine, ought to be a likely candidate.

Millinocket was for decades a thriving paper mill town, until Great Northern Paper ceased operations in 2008. Its fenced-off property sits abandoned, and although there's a growing outdoor recreation sector in the town of 4,100, its economy has struggled ever since.
Then came a plan, backed in part by Norwegian investors, for a $300 million US aquaculture venture repurposing the giant lagoons on the old mill site, to be called Great Northern Salmon.
"It was a marriage made in heaven," said Gail Fanjoy, the president of the local chamber of commerce. "Out of the gate, they were going to employ 50 people. That's a home run."

The project was about 80 per cent toward completion when the company announced last month it was pausing indefinitely, resting blame squarely on the uncertainty caused by the Trump administration's tariffs. Much of its salmon farming equipment was to be imported from Canada.
"That was a huge, huge, huge blow," Fanjoy told CBC News. "The Norwegian investors just said, 'We're done, we just can't deal with this.'"
Fanjoy, a lifelong resident of Millinocket, says nothing will make her believe Trump's claim that his trade policy will revive manufacturing in places like this.
"It's a fallacy," she said. "Paper companies all up and down the Penobscot River and the state of Maine closed, went bankrupt, and a tariff is not going to bring them back."
Cross-border trade matters to Maine
Maine does $6 billion US in annual two-way commerce with Canada — a significant amount in a state that's less populous than Manitoba.
The trade war is playing out amid a tight race for U.S. Senate in Maine, an election that will help determine which party controls Congress for the second half of Trump's term.

Maine's incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is something of a political phenomenon. The Republican has held her seat for the past 30 years in a place that hasn't voted statewide for a GOP presidential candidate since 1988.
If the Democrats are to win a majority in the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, Maine is a seat they'll almost certainly need to flip.
One big question in the race is if Maine voters will punish Collins as a proxy for their antipathy to Trump, whether over the trade war or other issues.
Tim Woodcock, a Bangor lawyer and a staunch backer of Collins, says many businesses have been adversely affected by tariffs, including those on Canadian products.

"These two economies are deeply intertwined," Woodcock told CBC News. "Anybody who is either trying to conduct a business in Maine or is dependent on a business in Maine would be very concerned about all the uncertainty that these tariffs have imposed."
'Canada's our friend'
CBC News spoke with Collins on the weekend as she walked in a parade in Carmel, a town of about 2,900.
Asked how concerned she is that Trump's tariffs will hurt her re-election chances, the 72-year-old senator parried the question.

"I'm much more concerned about the impact on the people of Maine in general. Many of our products, whether it's blueberries or potatoes or timber or lobster, are harvested here but processed in Canada," Collins said.
"Canada's our friend, our neighbour, our biggest trading partner," she added. "I urge the administration to get back to the table and both sides should engage in negotiations."
Among the townspeople lining the parade route was Chris Morang, who shook hands with Collins.
"I love her. She's always voted for helping the people in Maine. She's kept a lot of the hospitals going. She helped the lobster industry a lot," Morang told CBC News.
Although Collins has opposed Trump's trade war, Morang sides with the president.

"I think Canada has taken advantage of the United States a lot," he said. "They had unfair tariffs on us for many, many years, especially on lobster and lumber. I think at this point we're just getting what we deserve."

items: Republican senator warns Carney against tightening Canada's links to European Union

blocks.text: Collins has often tried to distance herself from Trump and his tariffs.

She was one of only seven Republican senators who voted to convict Trump in his impeachment trial for his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol. Last week, she supported a resolution calling for an end to the war with Iran.
Collins claimed victory this month when the White House lifted tariffs on two imports that Maine relies on from Canada: cement and road salt.
Her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, says tariffs are crushing Maine and he's dismissive of Collins' approach.
'Concerned letters' to Trump
"Everything costs more for people, and you can tell it's a big deal because Susan Collins was writing concerned letters to Donald Trump," Jackson told CBC News.
"She got us rock salt back, but we can't eat that."

items: The incoming U.S. import bans on Canadian alcohol, whey, molasses and motorcycles, by the numbers

blocks.text: Both Collins and Jackson grew up in northern Maine, each within a half hour's drive of the Canadian border. But that's where the similarities end.

Collins comes from a prosperous family who owned a lumber yard, and now has a net worth as high as $9.6 million US, according to a Democratic Party analysis of her Congressional financial disclosures.

Jackson was a logger and union activist who jumped into local politics after participating in a border blockade protesting companies bringing lower-paid Canadian loggers into Maine in the late 1990s. If he wins, he'll become the only sitting U.S. senator without a four-year college degree.
During a weekend town hall in the small coastal city of Belfast, Jackson wore a ball cap while talking proudly of his roots in northern Maine and his two decades in local politics.
Jackson replaced Graham Platner

"I speak funny, I know that. I didn't go to the right schools and all that. But what I think people have come to understand is that I am 100 per cent dug in on getting shit done," Jackson said to whoops and cheers from the audience.
Jackson only became the Democrat candidate in July after the original nominee Graham Platner stepped down when a former partner accused him of sexual assault.
John Luft, who came to the town hall from the nearby coastal town of Lincolnville, says Jackson is different from the typical political candidate.
"He actually speaks to what Mainers need right now. He actually gets it," Luft said.
Luft calls the trade war with Canada atrocious.
"I see no reason for this at all," he said. "Canada and United States have been friends forever and that's the way it should be."
Canadian companies have major investments in Maine, notably New Brunswick's Irving family empire with interests in logging, forest products and petroleum.

items: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump

blocks.text: Despite what polling suggests is widespread opposition to Trump's tariffs among Maine voters, it's only one of the issues at play in the election contest between Jackson and Collins.

Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine Farmington, says while both candidates have staked out positions against the trade war, Collins can pitch Mainers on her influence in Washington as a veteran senator and her record of defying Trump.
"In some ways, how this (trade war) has played out may favour her more than Jackson," Melcher told CBC News.
At the same time, Collins is seeking a sixth term from an electorate that Melcher describes as weary of the status quo.

"Certainly Troy Jackson is different, more blue collar, has a different approach to things," he said. "The perception of the economy and the national Republicans, I think, isn't helpful to [Collins] either."

items: Will the U.S. midterm results affect Trump's tariffs on Canada? Democrats think yes
Maine governor says her state is ‘not the enemy’ in ongoing trade war

blocks.text: Woodcock, the lawyer in Bangor, remains optimistic about Collins' re-election chances given what he calls the long tradition of independent judgment shown by Maine voters.
"They have tended to support, I'd say, the candidates who are willing to reach across the aisle, who are prepared to put the merits of an issue ahead of party," said Woodcock.

In her last election in 2020, Collins defied the anti-Trump wave. Despite polls that suggested she was poised to lose, she defeated her Democrat challenger by nine percentage points. She was the only Republican Senate candidate in the country to win in a state that voted for Joe Biden.

articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
articles.summary: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.

blocks.text: Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.
The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year.
Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December.
It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently.
But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough.
China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing.
Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs.
The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028.
What is striking is what was left out.
There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased.
The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping.
According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution.
After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack.
He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue.
This time, Trump disclosed far less.
"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend.
"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel."
That silence may be significant.
Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months.
Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit.
The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so.

Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations.
The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it.

Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed.
Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen.
And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans.

Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention.
So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place.

articles.title: Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen
articles.summary:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm

In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the…
articles.byline: Nasser al-Sakkaf in Taiz and William Christou

blocks.text: In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.

As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

“We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.”
He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies.

Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west, seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast.
The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen, with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022.

The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles.

Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air.
He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemenis carry water back to their makeshift camps. Photograph: Ebrahim Al-Suhaibi/Reuters

blocks.text: “Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.”

His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day.
“What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said.

Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students.

“On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said.

The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic.

“The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour.

blocks.caption: Children at al-Farsi camp for internally displaced people in southern Yemen. Photograph: Mohamad Hakim/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses.
Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people.

“It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods.

The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen.

“This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”

articles.title: Venezuelans demand opposition leader Machado's return
articles.summary: Hundreds of people held rallies in Venezuela demanding the safe return of Maria Corina Machado, and fair elections.

image.caption: Supporters of opposition leader Maria Corina Machado demanded her safe return to VenezuelaImage: Pedro Mattey/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Supporters of Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado held a rally on Sunday demanding her safe return and for fair presidential elections in Venezuela.
Her supporters joined the rally wearing sky-blue shirts which is the color of Machado's Vente Venezuela party and rode motorcycles through the streets in Caracas.
Similar rallies were held in several state capitals including Valencia, Maracaibo and Merida.
"This is not a matter of parties or politics," said Flavio Valentini, a Vente Venezuela activist in Caracas who grabbed a megaphone and addressed the crowd.

blocks.caption: Machado's supporters rode motocycles through streets as they demanded a free and fair election in VenezuelaImage: Juan Carlos Hernandez/REUTERS

blocks.text: "This is a movement for the people and by the people."
The demonstrators demanded a clear timeline for presidential elections in 2027 and chanted slogans including "Freedom, freedom!"
Machado's return from exile

For the past nine months, Machado has been living in exile. Last year in December, Machado left for Oslo to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Since then she has tried returning to Venezuela multiple times.
Machado, who is currently in Panama, has so far made seven unsuccessful attempts to return, according to media reports.
Activists allege the Venezuelan government keeps blocking her return, however, Venezuelan authorities deny the claim.
Venezuelans want elections — but when will they get them?
Courts had barred Machado from running in elections under the government of President Nicolás Maduro. But her stand-in candidate is widely believed to have won the election.

Maduro refuted the election results. After his disputed victory, his government led a crackdown against dissidents who protested the official results, forcing Machado and dozens of opposition leaders to flee.
The US captured Maduro in January. But Machado has been unable to return to Venezuela since then.
Currently, the country is being led by acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who has worked closely with Washington.

"We hope this transition process leads us to presidential elections and consolidates a free, democratic country that will be the main ally of the United States," said Anthony Romero, a leader for Vente Venezuela in the nation's capital.

articles.title: What would Francis of Assisi make of his fame today?
articles.summary: The Catholic saint renounced wealth and fame to become a mendicant friar. Yet over history, his teachings and life have inspired popes, Dante, and even Mussolini.

image.caption: Francis of Assisi is best known for his teachings about humankind's deep kinship with the natural world and non-human creaturesImage: picture alliance / Heritage Images

blocks.text: One could safely say that Francis of Assisi's life — and afterlife — is defined by paradox.
He embraced poverty, yet lies entombed today in a grand basilica with frescoes by renowned medieval artists in his native Assisi in central Italy.
He advocated meekness, yet hundreds of thousands venerated his remains when they went on public display earlier this year to commemorate 800 years since his death on October 3, 1226.

blocks.caption: Thousands came to venerate the saint's remains earlier this year, amid wide media coverage Image: Emanuela Bianconi/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: So, why has this Catholic saint inspired papal encyclicals, ecological activism, global pet‑blessing rituals — and even the propaganda of former Italian fascist leader Benito Mussolini?
And what might Francis make of this fame that he'd shunned while alive?
From riches to rags

Born in Assisi — a hill town in central Italy — in 1181 or 1182, he was first named Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone. But his father, a cloth merchant with trade links to France, renamed him Francesco.

Early Franciscan hagiographers — medieval writers who recorded his life and shaped how later generations understood him — describe him as a lively, sociable young man who enjoyed singing, parties and the privileges of wealth.

blocks.caption: The magnificent interior of the Basilica of St Francis of AssisiImage: Sepp Spiegl/IMAGO

blocks.text: However, he didn't want to join his father's trade; he dreamed of becoming a knight.

In 1202, Francis joined Assisi's forces in a battle against neighboring Perugia. He was captured, spent a year in prison, and returned home shaken and ill. This, and a series of subsequent events, precipitated a slow shift in his outlook.

One took place at the small, ruined Church of San Damiano outside Assisi, where Francis believed he heard Jesus Christ calling on him to "rebuild my church." Taking it literally, he began repairing local chapels. And when he ran out of money, he sold cloth from his father's shop, which enraged the latter and led to a dramatic episode in Assisi's town square.

blocks.caption: Norberto Proietti's 'The Return of St Francis' captures the saint returning as a dejected knight after his imprisonment in PerugiaImage: Gabriele Thielmann/imageBROKER/IMAGO

blocks.text: Before the bishop and gathered townspeople, Francis stripped off his fine clothes, renouncing his father, his inheritance and all material comforts. He committed himself to a life of poverty, humility, care for the poor and sick, and a deep kinship with nature.
A relatable saint
As a wandering preacher, he drew followers and eventually founded the Order of Friars Minor, known today as the Franciscans.

Widely considered the first saint to have miraculously received the stigmata — physical wounds resembling those on the crucified body of Jesus Christ — Francis was canonized by Pope Gregory IX on July 16, 1228. This unusually swift recognition amplified his fame beyond Assisi.

In the following centuries, Francis became one of the most frequently depicted saints in Western art, inspiring works from Dante's "Divine Comedy" to films, children's books, and even a 1980 Marvel comic.

blocks.caption: Cover of the 1980 Marvel comic on Francis' lifeImage: Marvel Comics Group

blocks.text: "Most saints are seen as unapproachable or unrelatable, but Francis' story of lifelong conversion and the desire to be in a positive relationship with others, God and the rest of creation speaks to people across time and cultures," theologian and former Franciscan friar Daniel P. Horan tells DW.

According to cultural historian Amanda Minervini, this broad appeal is also what made Francis so adaptable across eras: "In Francis, there seems to be something for everyone: the pacifist, the ascetic, the mason, the environmentalist, the minimalist, the lover of animals also loved by animals, the diplomat, the mystic, the radical, the performer, and even the model of a different kind of masculinity," they tell DW.

blocks.caption: Painting depicting Francis receiving the stigmata — the wounds of the crucified Jesus ChristImage: Heritage Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Pacifist mascot of a fascist regime

His image has been reconstructed throughout history, points out Minervini, who has explored in their research one particularly jarring example: Francis' political appropriation by Benito Mussolini's fascist regime.

In their recent book, "St. Francis and Mussolini: Fascist Appropriations of a Beloved Italian Saint" (2026), they explain how fascist rhetoric manipulated Francis' stigmata, reframing them as symbols of heroic suffering and sacrifice. "The wounds of the saint were thus invoked to glorify sacrifice and inspire Italian youth to go to war."

Noting how Mussolini chose to be rebaptized in 1927 to strengthen his alliance with the Vatican, they add, "St. Francis offered a particularly useful means of conferring religious legitimacy upon political power."

blocks.caption: Italian leader Benito Mussolini (left), who in fact inspired Germany's Adolf Hitler, appropriated Francis' teachings to legitimize fascist idealsImage: United Archives International/IMAGO

blocks.text: Minervini's research shows that Francis' pacifism — "likely because he had known what war meant" — was deliberately played down. Their book reproduces a confidential note addressed to military chaplains in 1929, which expressed concern that they might preach ideals of peace to the troops.
"This document provides clear evidence that peace was an aspect of Francesco's legacy that fascist groups sought to suppress rather than promote."

Furthermore, after Italy — a former Axis power along with Nazi Germany — switched sides and joined the Allies during World War II, the latter were often willing to condone or overlook Italy's crimes rather than investigate its fascist past.
"In this climate, many fascists remained in place, and the politically compromised image of Francis was quietly set aside," explains Minervini.

blocks.caption: Painting depicting St Francis having an audience with Sultan Malik al-KamilImage: IMAGO/Heritage Images

blocks.text: Medieval peace envoy
Francis has however remained associated with peace-making.

In 1219, during the Fifth Crusade, he traveled with the crusading army to Damietta, a port city in northern Egypt, and obtained permission to cross into the Muslim camp and meet personally with the sultan, Malik al-Kamil. His aim was to convert the sultan and bring an end to the bloody conflict.

Describing his action as "an extraordinarily audacious thing to do," Minervini says the encounter did not produce the conversion or political breakthrough Francis may have hoped for, but his return unscathed ensured that early sources took notice of him.

Daniel Horan adds that despite Christians viewing Muslims as the enemy back then, St Francis "would not go along with that dehumanizing perspective" and instead celebrated "the shared humanity and brotherhood he recognized in the Sultan."

blocks.caption: 2019 picture of the saint's namesake, Pope Francis, meeting Swedish climate activist, Greta Thunberg (holding poster), at St Peter's Square Image: picture alliance / abaca

blocks.text: From mendicant friar to climate icon
But he is most widely known as an animal lover and an early figure of environmental consciousness.

"He was ahead of his time both theologically and in terms of modern natural sciences, recognizing the complexity of the cosmos and the fact that human beings are also creatures in relationship with the world around us," says Daniel Horan, author of "Francis of Assisi and the Future of Faith" (2012).
In 1979, Pope John Paul II declared Francis the patron saint of ecology, while the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio chose the saint as his papal namesake when he became Pope Francis in 2013.

blocks.caption: Copies of Pope Francis' encyclical 'Laudato Si'' or 'Praise be to you' based on St Francis' 'Canticle of the Creatures' Image: imago/ZUMA Press

blocks.text: This pope would later publish "Laudato Si'" in 2015 — based on the saint's 1225 hymn "Canticle of the Creatures," in which he addresses natural elements as "Brother Sun," "Sister Moon" and "Sister Mother Earth."

The pope's encyclical connected environmental destruction directly to human suffering, besides critiquing consumerism and the "throwaway culture," and urging humanity to undergo an "ecological conversion."

"I also believe that in a time of deep polarization and economic inequality that St Francis models another way of being in the world, one that prioritizes relationship and community over individual gain and power," says Horan.

blocks.caption: St Francis' annual feast day on October 4 is also when pets are blessed, as seen here in a church in MumbaiImage: picture alliance / Sipa USA

blocks.text: But what might Francis make of his fame today?

"It's always tricky to try and guess what St. Francis, who died 800 years ago this October, would think about anything today. Our world is so unlike his own. But we do know that in his own time he was very uncomfortable with the positive reception he and his brother friars were receiving across Europe," says Horan.
Minervini suggests that he might have been more comfortable with representations of himself as a pacifist saint.

"I suspect he would be profoundly troubled, perhaps even furious, as it is known he could get upset, by the condition of our late-capitalist, technocratic world and by the ways in which we continue to understand ourselves as separate from, and superior to, the other creatures."

articles.title: Ed Miliband to acknowledge Labour’s former stance on Palestine fell short
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary will tell party’s conference ‘we are not here to accept the status quo but to change it’

Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of Palestinians they were right that Labour’s approach had not been enough, saying he was heeding the calls of millions of people by imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements.

The foreign secretary will tell the Labour party conference that the government will take more explicitly progressive foreign policy positions under Andy Burnham, and that the UK will be a leader among like-minded countries in a new age of diplomacy.

He will say there is a “fundamental and wider lesson from Israel and Palestine about how we have changed our approach as a party”, saying Labour will succeed “because of, not in spite of, our progressive values”.
He will talk of the start of a new and more muscular foreign policy. “We are not here to accept the status quo but to change it at home and abroad,” he will say.
The party’s conference hall was often the scene of fierce opposition to Keir Starmer’s stance on Israel and Palestine in Labour’s final year of opposition and early in government.

blocks.caption: The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images

blocks.text: Since becoming foreign secretary, Miliband has announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 countries – including France and Canada – announcing they would also impose sanctions.
The Guardian understands Miliband will say in his speech that the sanctions marked a definitive change in how Labour will approach the situation in the Middle East.
“I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right,” he will say.

“And under Andy’s leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions.
after newsletter promotion

“We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government, says ‘we will not let you succeed’.”

Miliband will pay tribute to those who have campaigned against the Israeli onslaught in Gaza, though his warm words are likely to raise questions about whether the government will review the proscription of Palestine Action. Police arrested a number of demonstrators outside the conference hall on Sunday.
“The bonds of solidarity between the British people and those who yearn for peace in Israel and Palestine are too strong to be broken,” Miliband will say.
“Our decision to act mobilised the international community, country after country. This is how to make change happen in today’s world. Doing what is right and galvanising others to act too.”

Miliband will say in his first speech to the party conference as foreign secretary that cooperation in imposing sanctions will be the beginning of a new bond with “likeminded countries” such as France and Canada, though it is also likely to be interpreted as being more willing to sideline the US.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has made an explicit argument for middle powers to do more to build alliances with each other outside traditional structures, and was direct in his desire to forge closer ties with and among European countries in a speech in Brussels earlier this month.

A source close to Miliband said that would be a key theme of his time in office. “Britain’s interests are served by standing up for our values on the world stage. Our ability to build coalitions on big global issues depends on our ability to bring countries with us,” he will say.
“This Israel/Palestine reset is a sign of how we want to do business. We are going to be propositional in bringing countries with us on the issues we really care about.”

articles.title: Ukraine, South Korea relations sour over North Korean POWs
articles.summary: South Korea has accused Ukraine of breaching a confidentiality agreement over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war — and of denying the deal's existence. Seoul has demanded an apology.

image.caption: 'I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing,' said Lee Jae MyungImage: Anthony Wallace/AFP

blocks.text: South Korea has demanded an official apology from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of breaching — and then reportedly denying the existence of — a confidentiality agreement regarding the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul.
Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer in an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, adding that the soldiers were "not easy to capture alive."
Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wrote on social media: "I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing."
On Sunday, the South Korean consternation was made official when Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, demanded "an official explanation and apology."

"The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine's unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement," Seong said in a statement.
"It is in itself a very serious matter that … seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries."
Seong said Seoul was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter," but did not specify what they might be.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
Ukraine: When were the North Korean soldiers captured?

The North Korean soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025 — two of around 14,000 North Korean troops deployed to the area to help halt and push back a surprise Ukrainian incursion.

Ukrainian intelligence estimates that around 3,000 North Korean troops were killed and another 1,500 injured, with the rest still stationed on Russian territory. To date, no North Korean troops are believed to have operated on Ukrainian territory itself.
Ukrainian troops reported that North Korean soldiers who were surrounded or injured on the battlefield preferred to die by suicide than surrender — and only two were captured.

Under President Lee, who has attempted to improve relations with the North, South Korea has appeared hesitant to take custody of the pair. But, under Article 3 of the South Korean constitution, North Koreans are still considered citizens of the South and are permitted to live in the South.
South Korea is an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which has so far only provided non-lethal aid. But Kyiv has been pressing Seoul to provide advanced air defense systems.
Last month, President Zelenskyy claimed that up to 50,000 more North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia.
Kim hails troops returning from Russia

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

Baste Duterte yet to say if he would appear at impeachment trial today
The Senate impeachment court has subpoenaed Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte from Monday, September 28, to Wednesday, September 30, 2026.
However, Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Alfred Corpuz says Duterte did not inform the court if he would appear at the trial on Monday.
Corpuz also says there will be no changes in the security protocols in the Senate.
Duterte was issued with a subpoena to testify in the impeachment trial of his older sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 23, lowers the voting threshold for conviction in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, changing the number of votes needed based on the senator-judges eligible to participate in the proceedings.
Rappler multimedia reporter Dwight de Leon explains how the ruling could affect the prosecution and defense, the possible new conviction threshold, and how both sides reacted to the decision.

blocks.text: Sep 23, 2026 9:07 PM PHT
Litigator counters Poa’s argument against lowering voting threshold

“Moving the threshold in terms of impeachment because it serves accountability does not have to mean moving the threshold elsewhere — bogeyman ‘yun,” litigator and Free Legal Assistance member Raffy Aquino said in a Rappler panel discussion during Day 29 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Wednesday, September 23.

The comment was made following defense lawyer Michael Poa’s argument that lowering the voting threshold for impeachment could have consequences on other constitutional provisions, such as revoking or extending martial law, expulsion of a member of the Senate, or amending the Constitution itself. – Rhen Peñada
Sep 23, 2026 8:54 PM PHT
A Villar split: Why is Mark Villar breaking ranks with sister Camille?
Two roads diverged in the Senate on Wednesday, September 23 — and the Villar siblings took different ones.

Senator-judge Mark Villar broke ranks with his sister, Senator-judge Camille Villar, and the Senate minority bloc in a surprise vote on two key motions during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Sep 23, 2026 7:36 PM PHT
Change in voting threshold not yet a ‘justiciable controversy’

Litigator and Free Legal Assistance Group member Raffy Aquino stressed on Wednesday, September 23, that the change in the voting threshold for the impeachment trial does not yet present a “justiciable controversy” that could be reviewed by the Supreme Court (SC).
“There is no injury yet. The Vice President still remains as vice president. And there is no vote yet on the conviction or acquittal,” he explained.
Aquino added that while the SC’s power of judicial review has been expanded to preserve its checking function, it remains limited and requires an actual controversy and grave abuse of discretion.
He added that if the previous threshold of 16 votes is still met, “then there is no controversy” since the conviction would stand.

Based on his experience as an “occasional constitutional litigator,” Aquino said the SC “does not easily lend itself to obstructions,” emphasizing that there must first be an actual controversy before the Court could intervene. – Rena Eñano
Sep 23, 2026 6:14 PM PHT
Why did Mark Villar vote differently from sister Camille?

Following the Senate impeachment court vote on the conviction voting threshold, litigator Raffy Aquino says on Wednesday, September 23, that the Villar siblings Mark and Camille showed one of two things: they either “demonstrated how it is to vote according to one’s conscience,” or it was a strategy to have a foot on either side of the door.

articles.title: France’s far-right National Rally surges in Senate elections
articles.summary:
Marine Le Pen hails ‘historic victory’ as her party and allies win enough seats to form caucus just months ahead of presidential poll

France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and its…

blocks.text: France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and its allies have secured a record 14 seats in the rightwing-dominated Senate in elections, effectively quadrupling its number in the 348-seat chamber just months before a presidential poll.
RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen called the results an “historic victory” after they were announced on Sunday. “The results ‌have exceeded our expectations,” she said.
It was the first time the ⁠party had cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a Senate caucus.
Local elected officials vote for new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term.
The far-right party entered the Senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the National Front, and won three seats in 2023.
Le Pen is considering her best chance yet at power in elections scheduled for a first round in April next year when the centrist president, Emmanuel Macron, steps down.
“This is a historic victory, and a major milestone with the formation for the first time of a group in the Senate,” she said on X.
Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, according to an AFP tally of results, on top of the three who won seats in 2023.
A further two were elected from RN ally Eric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party.
RN’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the party’s senators would form a group with UDR allies.

blocks.caption: RN president Jordan Bardella (C) poses with supporters in La Seyne-sur-Mer, southern France, on Sunday as the far right won a record 14 seats in Senate elections. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ciotti quit the rightwing Republicans (LR) party in 2024 after calling for an alliance with the far right.
The upper chamber’s LR president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, is expected to be re-elected next week.
The right, centre and leftwing Socialists looked set to remain the three major forces in the upper house, according to initial results.
The hard-left France Unbowed party won a seat for the first time.
Le Pen’s anti-immigration party emerged as the single largest party in the lower-house National Assembly after Macron called snap polls in 2024, although it fell well short of a majority.
With Reuters

articles.title: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
articles.summary:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while…

blocks.text: Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn, after a record multi-billion dollar deal was unveiled in December last year.

Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.

Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.

After Purdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times that the US had no plans to sell arms to China, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
Before the interview, Taiwanese deputy foreign minister Chen Ming-chi spoke of the severe military threat China posed.

“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.
Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.
Perdue himself told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.
With Reuters

articles.title: Israel strips Dutch diplomats of status in West Bank
articles.summary: The move by the Israeli Foreign Ministry is a response to Dutch sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The Dutch Foreign Ministry is yet to comment.

image.caption: 'Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it,' Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social mediaImage: Sebastian Christoph Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Israeli government said on Sunday that it was revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats representing The Netherlands at the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, the administrative capital of the Palestinian Territories.
Israeli ​Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the move was a response to Dutch sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
"Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it," Saar wrote on social media.
He ordered Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah to ​return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days.
"After this period, the diplomatic privileges and immunities granted to them by the State of Israel will expire," he added.
Israeli settlement trade ban widens across Europe
Dutch ban on settlement goods: what does it entail?
Dutch authorities announced earlier this month that they would begin enforcing a ban on settlement goods.

The ban, which applies to personal baggage as well as commercial shipments, came into force on September 22 and, in recent days, Dutch and Israeli media have reported that passengers arriving at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport from Israel had their luggage searched for banned goods.

Earlier in September, Israel also ordered the closure of ⁠the British Consulate ⁠in East Jerusalem, the United Kingdom's representative to the Palestinian Authority, after London announced similar sanctions banning the import of goods from illegal settlements.
"Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region," said Saar.
France and Canada have also announced a ban on goods from settlements, but Israel has not yet taken any action against ​those two countries.
In August, Israel also banned Dutch diplomats from a Israeli-based, US-led coordination center for Gaza over what the foreign minister described as "anti-Israel measures."
Israel pushes illegal West Bank settlement to record numbers

articles.title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day boss
articles.summary: World News Day aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.

blocks.text: World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.

It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer".
Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said.

In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom, external also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news.

But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said.
Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond.
"The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said.

"If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill."
Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society.
"We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said.
"We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts."
The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media".
Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us."

articles.title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91
articles.summary:
Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York

Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king…

blocks.text: Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.
Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.
His death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.
“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.

blocks.caption: Mighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Photograph: Frans Schellekens/Redferns

blocks.text: The Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso from Trinidad and Tobago to the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.
Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.

Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.

Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.
Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.
“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.
Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.

articles.title: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
articles.summary: In a system often marked by red tape and exhausting delays, officers seen to be following the rules get adulation.

blocks.text: Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years.
Tukaram Mundhe, 51, is one of them.

The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food.
He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged.

These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state.
Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments.
But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs?

In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post.
So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic.
"What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal.
For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds.
Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that.
One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules.

Kiran Bedi, the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported, external his decision).

Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020.
These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare.
Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention.
"Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible."
For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process.
Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints.
"What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says.
But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities.

Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases.

Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules.

Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay.
This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh.
Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties.

Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands.
"They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says.
She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper.
Jaswal remembers facing such pressure himself.
In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election.
He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after".
But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye.
The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward.
Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says.
Social media has also changed how quickly an officer can become a public sensation.
An action once limited to a district can now be filmed, shared and viewed by millions within hours.
"Social media can turn an official into a national talking point almost overnight," Sundar says.
That is partly what happened with Mundhe, whose inspection videos have turned routine enforcement into a widely watched spectacle.
Mundhe, however, sees it differently.
Speaking to the BBC last month, he said his actions were driven by public-health concerns and that businesses complying with rules had nothing to fear.
For Mundhe, the attention is beside the point. The rules already exist and his job is simply to enforce them.
But the public fascination is about more than just one officer.
When basic government functions are carried out visibly and consistently, they can seem extraordinary - particularly because so many people have come to expect otherwise.

articles.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo
articles.summary:
Hurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists

Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but…
